lenses.lens: SKILL CORPUS QUALITY — the 1,027 skill packages as a body of work
lenses.summary: The top ~85% of this corpus is genuinely excellent and does exactly what the owner wants: skills like security/data-classification-labels, admin/referral-management-health, and integration/loyalty-management-setup carry org-specific API names (CareProviderSearchableField), named permission-set licenses (Data Pipelines Base User), silent-failure modes, and LLM-failure-mode anti-patterns with detection hints — material an LLM's general training does not have. Structure is more consistent than expected (836/1027 use the same 9-section shape), triggers are genuinely natural-language (91% are 5+ words; 1,754 start with a question word), and description-level near-duplication is almost nil (3 pairs above 0.55 across 1,027). The problems are concentrated and fixable, not diffuse. A single 48-skill wave dated 2026-04-28 shipped stubs — 5-bullet llm-anti-patterns.md files as small as 178 bytes, examples.md with zero code — and several of those stubs are topic-duplicates of deep skills that already existed; I verified with search_knowledge.py that a 220-byte stub chunk ranks #1 for the exact query the 40 KB skill should own, which means the stubs actively poison retrieval rather than merely being dead weight. Beyond that: 15.0% of `## Related Skills` cross-references (339/2,253) point at skills that do not exist, 972/1,027 skills still declare `salesforce-version: "Spring '25+"` five releases after the fact, the corpus teaches the legacy `System.assertEquals` style 23:1 over the modern `Assert` class its own apex/test-class-standards skill mandates, and 71% of skill-local templates/ are byte-identical boilerplate. The validator's only depth gate is a 300-word minimum on SKILL.md body — nothing checks references/ substance, which is why the stub wave passed.

lenses.lens: AGENT LAYER — 47 active runtime agents, 14 build-time, 14 deprecated aliases; contract compliance, skill-coverage diff, new-agent proposals, alias hygiene, inputs schemas, overlap
lenses.summary: Structurally, the agent layer is in excellent shape: all 47 active runtime agents pass the 8-section AGENT_CONTRACT shape with correct ordering (scripted, zero exceptions), all 47 carry the Wave 10 persistence block and `default_output_dir`, 43/47 ship a typed-and-described `inputs.schema.json`, and the MCP router correctly excludes deprecated stubs. The headline coverage number is a mirage, though. A naive citation diff says 991/1027 skills (96.5%) are cited by some agent — but 495 of the 1,048 numbered "Mandatory Reads" entries are machine-generated echo stubs whose description is literally the slug with dashes replaced by spaces ("Fsl mobile app setup", "Npsp household accounts"). Counting only human-authored reads, just 488/1027 skills (47.5%) are reachable through an agent that actually needs them. The cause is mechanical: `_check_orphan_skills` in `validate_repo.py` emits an **ERROR** for any skill not listed in some agent's `dependencies.skills:`, with no cap on citations per agent, so the cheapest way to clear the gate is `patch_agent_skill.py` — and `object-designer` now carries 123 stub reads across 152 skills, directly violating AGENT_RULES.md Step 6's own "don't dilute Mandatory Reads" rule. Underneath the sweep sit six entire Salesforce verticals with no agent at all: OmniStudio/Industries (51 skills), CRM Analytics + Data Cloud (49), CPQ/Revenue (35), Field Service (24), Commerce (22), Marketing Cloud (22) — 203 skills, 20% of the library, unreachable by any agent. I confirmed the user-facing consequence empirically: `suggest_agent` misrouted 5 of 8 realistic vertical queries ("design an OmniScript" → `omni-channel-routing-designer`; "CPQ pricing rules" → `duplicate-rule-designer`) and never abstains. Secondary defects: 20 of 47 active agents recommend deprecated agents as follow-ups (`config-workbook-author` hard-codes five deprecated agents into its plan and would then refuse its own output via `REFUSAL_RECOMMENDED_AGENT_INVALID`), 33/47 have no eval baseline, and `flow-builder`/`changeset-builder` document input names that share zero overlap with their harness schemas.

lenses.summary: The content layer is strong and the machine-facing docs are unusually disciplined — `standards/validation-gates.md` is generated from validator source, README's per-domain skill counts are exactly correct (253/158/82/63/34/53/48/61/101/104/70 = 1027, verified), and `search_knowledge.py` returns a genuinely good first answer. The human-facing IA is where this fails. There is no getting-started path, no tutorial, and no worked end-to-end example anywhere in the repo; a new user lands on a 540-line README with no table of contents where "5-Minute Setup" sits at line 83 behind an advanced single-agent-export section, and MCP setup — the headline differentiator — is at line 477, *after* the maintainer sign-off at line 466. Worse, the two docs designated canonical contradict each other on a gate that hard-fails the build: `AGENT_RULES.md` says orphan skills are a WARN that "do not block the commit"; `CLAUDE.md` and the generated `standards/validation-gates.md` both say ERROR. `CONTRIBUTING.md` is three months stale — it still instructs contributors to add markdown table rows to `MASTER_QUEUE.md`, which has held no rows since 2026-05-01. README links `/run-queue` to a file that does not exist while the actual current entrypoint `/build-skills` and the flagship `/onboard-source` appear nowhere in README. Navigation for 1027 skills is one 587KB generated table with 14 headings and no anchors; eight major directories (`agents/`, `commands/`, `skills/`, `scripts/`, `standards/`, `knowledge/`, `exports/`, `config/`) have no README index at all.

lenses.summary: The engineering underneath distribution is genuinely good — 8 export targets all run in ~1.5s, `export_agent_bundle.py` produces an excellent 676K self-contained drop-in bundle, `--install` writes the correct cross-tool `.agents/skills/` + `.claude/skills` symlink layout, and CONNECT.md covers 16 MCP clients in 693 lines. But the last mile is broken in ways that would stop essentially every new user. The install path that CONNECT.md calls "recommended for end users" fails at both steps: `pip install sfskills-mcp` resolves an unpinned `mcp>=1.4.0` to mcp 2.0.0 and crashes on import, and `sfskills-mcp-init` HTTP 404s because the repo has zero GitHub releases despite a workflow that builds the data bundle for them. For Claude Code — the flagship target — a fresh clone contains exactly one tracked file under `.claude/` and the README's claim that "`.claude/commands/` ships in-tree" is false; the installer that would fix it is never mentioned in the README. There is no `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, so the now-native Claude Code distribution channel is entirely absent. Release discipline barely exists: 0 GitHub releases, 4 tags all MCP-scoped, no library version, and all 6 CHANGELOG headings still say "[Unreleased]". The single biggest friction is that there is no working one-command install for any tool — every documented path either crashes, 404s, requires a 131 MB clone plus undocumented manual steps, or dumps ~134K tokens of skill frontmatter into the user's context.

lenses.summary: The gate *design* here is genuinely strong — 68 indexed gates, a generated `standards/validation-gates.md` that is itself drift-checked, an agent-citation gate that resolves every skill/template/command/MCP-tool reference, and a fully-satisfied orphan gate (986 cited + 41 explicit orphans = 1027, zero silent). The *enforcement* is where it falls apart. `scripts/generate_queue_dashboard.py:279` stamps `date.today()` into a drift-checked artifact, so `validate_repo.py` has exited 1 on a clean tree every day since 2026-07-09 — the repo's own gate, its README badge, and every contributor's first command are permanently red for a two-line date diff. Because the baseline is always red, the gate cannot distinguish a broken PR from normal. Beyond that, the gates CI actually runs are a subset of the gates that exist: the 1,356-fixture retrieval-quality check (the gate that protects the core product promise — does the right skill get retrieved) runs in zero CI jobs and zero hooks, and 21 of 24 MCP test modules (233 of 248 tests, including the SOQL DML blocklist and secret redaction) never run. There are no unit tests at all for 16,866 lines of `scripts/` + `pipelines/`, and the one bench that claims to guard orchestration cost passes with 14x slack (500 synthetic skills in 2.16s) while a real 263-skill shard takes 130s. CONTRIBUTING.md has not been touched since the initial 77-skill commit and omits every gate added since — a human following it end-to-end hits hard ERRORs it never warned them about.

lenses.summary: The retrieval stack is well-engineered at the plumbing level (in-process SearchContext, FTS5 safety sanitizer, 100% fixture coverage across all 1027 skills, a config file that documents its own tuning experiments with measured numbers) but its published quality number is not measuring what users experience. I ran 36 hand-written natural-language queries a practitioner would actually type and adjudicated them myself: Hit@1 = 36.1%, Hit@3 = 50.0%, and 16.7% returned "Coverage: NONE" while the correct skill demonstrably existed and had already been ranked. The 98.6% headline comes from author-written trigger phrases fed back with the answer's own domain pre-supplied as a filter — I reproduced 97.0% with the domain and 94.8% without on 500 fixtures, confirming the corpus is self-referential rather than the harness being wrong. The single highest-leverage defect is that min_skill_score=1.5 is arithmetically unreachable for any skill matching one chunk (ceiling is 1.3 without a domain filter), so the engine reports "no coverage" for correct answers. Separately, evals are entirely aspirational: grep finds zero references to evals/ in .github/ or .githooks/, the retrieval fixture gate is disabled on all four CI shards behind a stale "Wave 6" comment, and one of the ten golden eval files points at a skill path that does not exist while --structure still reports [OK]. Embeddings are enabled in config, cost 8.3s load and 2.85GB RSS, contribute exactly 0.0pp (identical Hit@1/Hit@3 to three significant figures across 400 fixtures), and the shipped MCP server never uses them at all.

lenses.lens: External landscape and competitive positioning (2026 AI-assistant skill/context ecosystem)
lenses.summary: The product is technically ahead of every competitor on depth (1,027 packages averaging 62 KB / 9 files each, vs Salesforce's 112 single-file skills) and is the only Salesforce skill library shipping runtime agents, decision trees, golden evals and a live-org MCP server. It is losing badly on distribution: 9 stars vs forcedotcom/sf-skills' 778, zero presence in the registries that now drive discovery, and no `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` — the single mechanism Claude Code uses to install third-party skill collections in 2026. Two assumptions the repo is operating on are now factually wrong and both are load-bearing: (1) forcedotcom/sf-skills is Apache-2.0, not CC BY-NC, so the clean-room constraint is self-imposed overhead; (2) `npx skills add PranavNagrecha/AwesomeSalesforceSkills` already works and discovers all 1,027 skills, but the README mentions npx zero times. The structural blocker underneath everything is that installing the whole library as native Agent Skills costs ~134K tokens of startup metadata, so "1,027 skills" is simultaneously the headline claim and the reason nobody can install it — the library needs domain-sized plugin bundles the way wshobson/agents splits 175 skills into 94 plugins. Positioning should stop competing with Salesforce on generation breadth and claim the complementary half: SfSkills is the review, architecture and governance layer that installs *alongside* sf-skills, backed by an org-aware MCP server that checks the real org before recommending anything.

lenses.lens: Salesforce Platform Coverage Gaps (2026 platform surface vs. library inventory)
lenses.summary: The library's breadth on the *classic* platform surface is genuinely excellent — I hypothesized 22 gaps and 10 of them (45%) turned out to be real coverage I would have wrongly reported: Privacy Center (in `security/gdpr-data-privacy`), UTAM/Playwright/Selenium (in `devops/automated-regression-testing`), MIAW-vs-retired-Chat (`admin/messaging-and-chat-setup` correctly excludes legacy Live Agent), Code Analyzer **v5** (not v4), Tableau Pulse embedding, Agentforce Testing Center, Data Cloud zero-copy, Einstein Studio/Model Builder, headless identity, and Channel Revenue Management/rebates. Only 2 of ~30 `search_knowledge.py` probes returned a literal `Coverage: NONE`. The real risk is not absence, it is **currency and portfolio balance**: the library is a very good 2024–early-2025 snapshot that has not tracked the 2025–26 product pivots. 972 of 1027 skills declare `salesforce-version: "Spring '25+"`, only 23 SKILL.md files mention Spring '26 and 6 mention Summer '26, and 32 have a malformed version string. Concretely, that means: zero coverage of Agentforce Voice (GA in Spring '26), zero build coverage of Marketing Cloud Next / Growth / Advanced against 24 legacy MCE+Pardot skills, 18 Salesforce CPQ skills (end-of-sale March 2025) versus one file mentioning `ProductSellingModel`, and the skill whose entire job is "Salesforce Functions is retired, what next?" never mentions Heroku AppLink. A practitioner installing this today gets expert help on the platform Salesforce sold in 2024 and materially wrong or absent help on what Salesforce sells and demos in 2026.

lenses.lens: THE END-USER JOURNEY — DOES IT ACTUALLY WORK? (5 personas simulated against a fresh clone)
lenses.summary: I cloned the repo the way a new user would (`git clone --depth 1`) and drove all five personas through it. The content is genuinely strong — `standards/decision-trees/automation-selection.md` is better than most consulting decks, the runtime AGENT.md shape (`/preflight-load`, `/design-lead-routing`, `/refactor-apex`) has typed inputs and explicit non-goals, and every `templates/apex/*.cls` an agent cites actually exists. But the journey breaks before any of that is reachable. On a fresh clone the README's own demo command, `python3 scripts/search_knowledge.py "trigger recursion"`, returns "Coverage: NONE" — the retrieval index is gitignored (>50MB) and no setup step rebuilds it; the rebuild I ran was still producing zero output after 14m36s. The README also claims `.claude/commands/` "ships in-tree" while `.gitignore:63` excludes it, so a fresh clone has zero slash commands and the fix (`scripts/install_local_commands.py`) is documented only inside that script's own docstring. Discoverability then fails structurally: the index contains 130,062 chunks from `skills/` and `knowledge/` and **zero** from `agents/`, `commands/`, or `standards/decision-trees/`, so none of my five personas could find the agent built for their job — the consultant's "assess an unfamiliar org" query returned "Coverage: NONE" while `/assess-org` sat right there. The worst failure mode is inverted confidence: a fabricated product ("Salesforce Quantum Ledger blockchain object encryption") returned `security/platform-encryption` at score 3.073 with no caveat, while the real, well-covered "migrate 5 million records into Salesforce" returned "Coverage: NONE". This is a library that would impress a reviewer who reads it and frustrate a user who runs it.

lenses.summary: The *content* layout is genuinely excellent and the owner should stop worrying about it: all 1027 skill packages are byte-for-byte uniform (100% have `references/` + all four required reference files, `templates/`, `scripts/`), 0/1027 skill directories violate kebab-case, and `.gitignore` is one of the most carefully reasoned I've seen — every exclusion carries a comment explaining the regeneration command. The problem is everything *around* the content. The repo root has 28 directories and 14 files, of which 15 directories are undocumented in CLAUDE.md's own "Repository Structure" block; four separate Python venvs (222 MB), a 345 MB orphaned worktree tree, and 8 abandoned stashes sit in the working copy. Worst, `git clone` of `main` pulls 178 MB when the tracked working tree is only 33.5 MB — 137 MB of that is 518 dead versions of `vector_index/chunks.jsonl` that were gitignored in commit `59e265ce6` but never purged from history. And the single most-advertised install path is broken: README line 45 promises Claude Code users that `.claude/commands/` "ships in-tree", but `.gitignore:63` excludes it and `git ls-files .claude/` returns exactly one file — so a fresh clone gives a Claude Code user zero of the 65 slash commands, and the script that fixes it (`scripts/install_local_commands.py`) is referenced in zero markdown files in the repo. Three competing backlog documents live at root, and 142 dated session artifacts are tracked in `main` in direct violation of the repo's own stated rule.

confirmed_gaps.why_it_matters: `## Related Skills` is how an assistant chains from the skill it retrieved to the next one it needs. One in seven of those hops dead-ends. Worse, CLAUDE.md's own agent contract requires that 'every citation must resolve to a real skills/<domain>/<slug>/SKILL.md' — so an agent faithfully following a skill's Related Skills list will emit a citation that violates the repo's own rule. The 256 nonexistent slugs are also a free, evidence-backed backlog: they are the skills the corpus itself says it wants.
confirmed_gaps.proposed_fix: (1) Add `validate_related_skills_links` to pipelines/validators.py — ERROR on any `<domain>/<slug>` inside `## Related Skills` that does not resolve to skills/<domain>/<slug>/SKILL.md; register it in standards/validation-gates.md. (2) Auto-fix the 83 wrong-domain refs with a one-shot script (slug is unique, so the correct domain is derivable). (3) Dump the 256 nonexistent slugs, dedupe by frequency, and load the top ~40 into BACKLOG.yaml as evidence-backed skill candidates — the corpus has already told you what is missing.

refuted_claims.lens: SKILL CORPUS QUALITY — the 1,027 skill packages as a body of work
refuted_claims.title: The 48-skill stub wave of 2026-04-28 outranks the deep skills it duplicates in lexical retrieval
refuted_claims.reason:
Three of the claim's load-bearing assertions fail against the repo.

(1) THE HEADLINE "OUTRANKS" IS AN ARTIFACT OF UNSORTED PRINT ORDER. The claim's own pasted output shows `lwc/virtualized-lists (3.924)` printed above `lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists (4.580)` — the stub is listed first while scoring LOWER. scripts/search_knowledge.py:321-323 iterates payload["skills"] with no sort. Sorting the JSON by score puts the deep skill first at 4.580 vs 3.924. So at the skill-selection layer the deep skill already wins; only a single 220-byte chunk holds the top chunk slot, and the same result set surfaces four lwc-virtualized-lists chunks (scripts/check_lwc_virtualized_lists.py 0.594, examples.md 0.510, well-architected.md 0.460, gotchas.md 0.427). The deep skill is not being crowded out.

(2) THE FLOW EVIDENCE IS FABRICATED. The claim states the #1 chunk for "my flow is failing in production" is skills/flow/flow-interview-debugging/SKILL.md at 1.263. It is not. The #1 chunk is skills/flow/flow-large-data-volume-patterns/SKILL.md at 1.237; flow-interview-debugging is #2 at 0.747 — a different file rank and a score off by 0.516. Additionally the query returns `Coverage: NONE — no skill meets the confidence threshold` with an EMPTY Top-skills list, so neither the stub nor flow/flow-debugging is surfaced as a skill at all. Nothing is displacing anything.

(3) THE SIZE FIGURES ARE WRONG. Claim says lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists is 40,564 bytes and flow/flow-debugging is 38,508 bytes. Actual: the lwc-virtualized-lists .md files total 39,935 bytes (du 76 KB incl. scripts/templates); flow-debugging is 84 KB. Minor, but consistent with numbers not being re-measured.

WHAT IS REAL: 228 skills carry `updated: 2026-04-28`; 49 of them have an llm-anti-patterns.md under 700 bytes, and the stub shape is exactly as described (skills/lwc/virtualized-lists/references/well-architected.md is 533 bytes and its entire body before Official Sources is "**Performance:** constant memory + FPS. **UX:** scalable UI."). That is a genuine thin-content / near-duplicate finding worth filing — but as a corpus-quality defect, not a retrieval regression, and not P0. The "zero-sum 30-chunk window" argument is invoked without a measurement showing any skill actually fell below min_skill_score because of these stubs; in the one query where it could be checked, the deep skill still scored highest.
refuted_claims.corrected: A ~49-skill thin-content wave dated 2026-04-28 exists and is a real CONTENT-QUALITY problem (P2, not P0): 49 skills whose references/llm-anti-patterns.md is under 700 bytes (smallest 178 B, skills/flow/flow-interview-debugging), with two-sentence well-architected.md files and code-free examples.md. Several are near-duplicates of a deep skill (lwc/virtualized-lists vs lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists; flow/flow-interview-debugging vs flow/flow-debugging) and none of these pairs appear in docs/reports/duplicate-candidates.md, which was last generated filtered to `--domain devops` (68 skills only). The right fix is merge-or-rescope of the duplicate pairs and regenerating the duplicate audit across all domains. The retrieval-poisoning mechanism, however, does not hold: skill-level scoring — the primary output an agent acts on — already ranks the deep skill higher (lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists 4.580 > lwc/virtualized-lists 3.924); the stub only occupies one chunk slot, and the `Top skills:` print order in scripts/search_knowledge.py (lines 321-323) is unsorted, which is what makes the stub LOOK like it ranks first.

(2) REFUTED "structurally cannot see them": --threshold and --full-scan are CLI flags on scripts/audit_duplicates.py; the lwc-accessibility pair (0.403) surfaces at --threshold 0.40. (4) REFUTED "7 pairs where a 5-6 KB stub meets a 20-47 KB deep skill": only 3 pairs fit (virtualized-lists 5,629 vs 40,564; drag-and-drop 5,595 vs 20,435; flow-interview-debugging 5,429 vs 38,508). Measured: guest-user-security 27,889 vs guest-user-security-audit 24,053; architect/event-driven-architecture 51,205 vs integration/event-driven-architecture-patterns 50,670; apex/record-locking-and-contention 35,956 vs flow/flow-record-locking-and-contention 65,178; and apex/apex-managed-sharing 47,833 vs security/apex-managed-sharing-patterns 9,305 (size direction reversed from the claim). Several cross-domain pairs read as deliberate domain lenses, not shadow duplicates. (5) PARTIALLY SATISFIED: BACKLOG.yaml:199-206 already records flow-interview-debugging with status "DUPLICATE" and a triage note naming skills/flow/flow-debugging as the covering skill; 857 BACKLOG entries carry DUPLICATE status, and pipelines/validators.py:569 validate_skill_similarity is a live (WARN) gate. (6) Their own evidence output mislabels flow/flow-debugging as "lwc/flow-debugging". Not P0 — the corpus-quality cost is a handful of triage-worthy twins plus a missing slug signal, not a systemic blindness.

The rest are comparably-sized skills or deliberate cross-domain lenses. refuted_claims.lens: SKILL CORPUS QUALITY — the 1,027 skill packages as a body of work
refuted_claims.title: 94.6% of the corpus is pinned to a release stamp that is five Salesforce releases old, with 32 malformed values
refuted_claims.reason:
The headline distribution reproduces byte-for-byte (972/1027 = 94.65%, 32 malformed), so that arithmetic is real. But the framing and three of the four supporting statistics do not survive.

(1) MISCHARACTERIZED SEMANTICS. `salesforce-version` carries a `+` suffix — it is a MINIMUM-supported-release floor, not a currency stamp. "Spring '25+" asserts "applies to Spring '25 and later," which is still true in Summer '26. Calling it "pinned to a release stamp five releases old" inverts the field's meaning. It is also the literal canonical default: `config/skill-scaffold.md:5` and the required-frontmatter block in `CLAUDE.md:137` both ship `salesforce-version: "Spring '25+"`. 94.6% matching the scaffold default is the scaffold working, not corpus rot. A skill on trigger bulkification with a Spring '25 floor is not stale.

(2) NO GATE TREATS IT AS CURRENCY. `pipelines/validators.py:46-59` lists `salesforce-version` in REQUIRED_FRONTMATTER_KEYS — presence only. There is no value regex, no enum, no recency check anywhere in `scripts/validate_repo.py` or `pipelines/validators.py` (grep for stale|currency|retired|outdated returns only the generated-artifact staleness gate). So "the frontmatter schema apparently accepts" the malformed value is trivially true of ANY string; the schema was never claiming to validate it.

(3) THE MALFORMED VALUE IS COSMETIC, NOT BROKEN. `"Spring '25+'"` is valid YAML — a double-quoted scalar parsing to the string `Spring '25+'`. yaml.safe_load on flow/flow-bulkification returns it cleanly. Nothing crashes, nothing mis-indexes; 32 files carry a stray apostrophe. That is a P3 typo sweep, not P1.

(4) THE API-VERSION STAT IS WRONG BY ~8x. Claim: "only 16 references at v66/v67." Actual: 122 references across 23 skill directories.

(5) THE RELEASE-MENTION STATS ARE WRONG BY 3x AND 4x. Claim: "only 21 skills mention Summer '26" — actual 7 unique skill directories (26 files). Claim: "only 8 mention Winter '27" — actual 2 skill directories (architect/industries-integration-architecture, omnistudio/industries-api-extensions). Note these cut AGAINST the claimant on v66/v67 and FOR them on Summer '26/Winter '27, so this is sloppy counting in both directions, not a consistent bias.

What is genuinely actionable: normalize the 32 mismatched-quote values, and optionally add a value-shape regex to validators.py. That is a P3 hygiene item. The "five releases stale corpus" narrative is not supported.
refuted_claims.corrected: 32 of 1,027 SKILL.md files carry a stray trailing apostrophe in `salesforce-version` (`"Spring '25+'"` instead of `"Spring '25+"`). The value still parses as valid YAML and nothing consumes it semantically — `pipelines/validators.py:46` checks key presence only — so impact is cosmetic. Worth a one-line sed sweep plus an optional value-shape regex in the validator. P3. The broader "94.6% is stale" framing should be dropped: the `+` suffix makes the field a minimum-supported-release floor (Spring '25+ is still satisfied by Summer '26), and `"Spring '25+"` is the canonical scaffold default in `config/skill-scaffold.md:5` and `CLAUDE.md:137`, so near-universal agreement with it is expected, not decay.

refuted_claims.lens: SKILL CORPUS QUALITY — the 1,027 skill packages as a body of work
refuted_claims.title: The corpus teaches legacy Apex idioms 12:1 over the modern ones its own standard skill mandates
refuted_claims.reason:
Half the claim reproduces exactly; the other half is measurably backwards, and the severity is inflated.

WHAT VERIFIED (real, and actually stronger than they argued):
- Their command re-ran identically: 114 `System.assertEquals` vs 5 `Assert.areEqual` in skills/; 36 `System.assert(` vs 5 `Assert.isTrue|isNotNull` (they said 7 — minor overcount); `grep -rln 'Assert\.areEqual|Assert\.isTrue' templates/` returns nothing, and `grep -rn "Assert\." templates/` returns zero lines total. templates/apex/tests/BulkTestPattern.cls lines 24/35/49/62 confirmed.
- Only 2 files in the entire 1,027-skill corpus use any modern `Assert.*` method, and both are inside skills/apex/test-class-standards/ itself (SKILL.md + references/examples.md). 67 files use the legacy form.
- Two facts they missed that make the self-contradiction sharper: (a) skills/apex/test-class-standards/references/llm-anti-patterns.md uses `System.assertEquals` in its *corrected* "good" examples (lines 34, 71, 110, 194) and names it in a detection hint at line 75 — the file teaching the anti-pattern demonstrates the legacy idiom in its own fix; (b) standards/code-review-checklist.md:63 affirmatively mandates the legacy form: "**Meaningful assertions** — `System.assertEquals(expected, actual, 'message')` for every outcome". No validator or lint gate anywhere in scripts/, pipelines/, or .github/ checks assertion style.

WHY REFUTED AS STATED:
1. The security half is the opposite shape from what they claim. skills/ has 137 files with `WITH USER_MODE` vs 83 with `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` — the modern form is the 62% majority, not a legacy-dominated 12:1 ratio. Worse for their framing, 44 of those 83 SECURITY_ENFORCED files also contain USER_MODE (contrastive teaching of both, which is correct since SECURITY_ENFORCED is still supported and is the only option below API 55). Only 39 files are SECURITY_ENFORCED-only. Their own numbers (83 vs 137) show this and they still labelled it "same shape."
2. The 38/39 `isAccessible()` files are not evidence of legacy drift — describe-based FLS checks remain the required mechanism for DML and non-SOQL paths, which `USER_MODE` does not cover.
3. P1 is overstated. The skill they cite explicitly states, one sentence after the line they quote: "The legacy `System.assert`, `System.assertEquals`, and `System.assertNotEquals` methods remain supported with no announced retirement, so existing tests do not need a rewrite, but new tests should default to the `Assert` class." This is example-code style consistency, not a correctness, security, or deprecation exposure.
refuted_claims.corrected: Assertion-style drift is real but is a P2/P3 consistency defect, not P1, and it does not extend to security idioms. Accurate version: "skills/apex/test-class-standards/SKILL.md tells authors new tests should default to the `Assert` class, but the corpus contains only 2 files using any modern `Assert.*` method (both inside that same skill) against 67 files using `System.assertEquals`. templates/apex/tests/ — the canonical shared test templates — contain zero `Assert.*` calls, and standards/code-review-checklist.md:63 actively mandates the legacy `System.assertEquals(expected, actual, 'message')` form. The same skill's own llm-anti-patterns.md uses the legacy form in its corrected examples. Nothing in the validator enforces assertion style. Severity is bounded because the skill itself documents that the legacy methods remain supported with no announced retirement. refuted_claims.lens: SKILL CORPUS QUALITY — the 1,027 skill packages as a body of work
refuted_claims.title: 71% of skill-local templates/ are byte-identical zero-content scaffold, and 50 checker scripts only verify file existence
refuted_claims.reason: Their raw counts reproduce exactly (735 / 1037 / 50), but the inference from those counts is wrong. Grepping for "Request summary:" and "## Scope" matches the scaffold HEADER, which was kept even in templates that were later filled with real content — so the grep cannot distinguish an empty worksheet from a fully-authored one. Two independent measurements break the "byte-identical zero-content" characterisation: (1) after normalising away the skill slug, all 735 files hash uniquely — zero duplicates, so nothing is byte-identical; (2) line-count distribution of the 735 is min 27 / p25 32 / median 82 / p75 127 / p90 153 / max 292 — a 292-line file is not a "generic worksheet with the skill name substituted". Classifying by H2 heading-set signature gives the true figure: only 231 files (177 with `## Approach`, 54 with `## Selected Pattern`) have the pure scaffold shape, and every one of those is <=56 lines. The claim's own example (csp-and-trusted-urls, 27 lines) is a real member of that 231 — the example is valid, the extrapolation to 735 is not. The checker-stub finding is fully confirmed and unrefuted, but at 50/1057 it is a 4.7% tail, not a corpus-wide quality failure; the non-stub checkers median 200 lines.
refuted_claims.corrected: 231 of 1,037 skill-local template files (22%, not 71%) are genuine zero-content generic worksheets — identifiable by having ONLY the five scaffold H2s (`## Scope | ## Context Gathered | ## Approach|Selected Pattern | ## Checklist | ## Notes`), 27-32 lines, TODO placeholders. The other ~504 files that match the "Request summary:" grep carry substantial skill-specific Salesforce content under the same scaffold header (median 82 lines, p75 127, max 292) — e.g. skills/lwc/commerce-lwc-components/templates/commerce-lwc-components-template.md has a `commerce/productApi` / `commerce/cartApi` wire-adapter selection table and a `<capability>lightningCommunity__RelaxedCSP</capability>` meta-XML checklist. The checker-stub half of the claim is accurate but should be scoped: 50 of 1,057 skill checker scripts (4.7%) are 34-line existence-only stubs; the other 1,007 have median 200 lines (min 19, max 619) of real logic. Severity is P2, not P1 — the defect is ~22% of templates plus 4.7% of checkers, not "the majority".

refuted_claims.lens: SKILL CORPUS QUALITY — the 1,027 skill packages as a body of work
refuted_claims.title: The only quality gate is a 300-word minimum on SKILL.md body — nothing checks references/ substance, which is why the stub wave shipped
refuted_claims.reason:
The headline is factually wrong on two counts, and the claim contradicts itself in its own body.

(1) "The only quality gate is a 300-word minimum on SKILL.md body — nothing checks references/ substance" is FALSE. `pipelines/validators.py` lines 262-283 gate `references/llm-anti-patterns.md`: ERROR if missing (L265), ERROR on unfilled `TODO:` markers (L270), and a WARN if `_count_anti_patterns()` (L459-477, three regex formats, max-not-sum) returns < 5 (L279). Lines ~361-425 gate `references/well-architected.md` for a `## Official Sources Used` heading AND at least one non-empty line of content after it (ERROR), and flag verbatim paragraph duplication between SKILL.md and `references/gotchas.md` (ERROR, L421) and pillar-section duplication vs well-architected.md (ERROR, L376). All six of these are indexed in `standards/validation-gates.md` rows 35-43. The claimant's own grep was `grep -n "MIN_"` — a search for constant names, which structurally cannot find any gate that isn't implemented as a `MIN_*` constant. That is a search artifact, not a finding.

(2) "no check that llm-anti-patterns.md contains 5+ mistakes (CLAUDE.md requires '5+ mistakes')" is FALSE and is refuted by the claim's own next clause — "a 178-byte file of five 3-word fragments technically satisfies it" concedes the check exists and fires. The complaint is that the check is count-based rather than depth-based, which is a much narrower point than "nothing checks".

(3) The claim also misses `standards/skill-content-contract.md`, which is the repo's documented per-file depth standard: examples.md "Minimum examples: 2 complete examples" with a required Scenario/Problem/Solution/Why-it-works/Source structure and a mandatory failure example; gotchas.md "Minimum gotchas: 3 entries"; well-architected.md "At least 1 pillar addressed with specific guidance (not just naming the pillar)"; plus a severity table (L241-243) that grades "examples.md has fewer than 2 complete examples" and "gotchas.md has fewer than 3 entries" as HIGH / Block commit. That file even names its own division of labour at L263: "`scripts/validate_repo.py` Enforces structural gates. This contract enforces quality gates that scripts cannot check." So the requirement is written down and severity-ranked; it is deliberately delegated to the authoring/review agent rather than to regex.

What survives: there is genuinely no *automated* length or depth floor on any references/ file, the 5+ anti-pattern check is count-only and WARN-level (non-blocking), and `skills/flow/flow-interview-debugging` does pass clean (validated in the 63-skill flow domain run; the 11 errors emitted are all `check_doc_counts` 47-vs-48 runtime-agent drift, none from that skill). That is a real but much smaller gap than "the only quality gate is 300 words".
refuted_claims.corrected: Automated depth enforcement on references/ files is count-based, not substance-based — and the 5+ anti-pattern check is WARN-level, so it never blocks. `pipelines/validators.py` DOES gate references/ (L265 missing-file ERROR, L270 TODO-marker ERROR, L279 <5 anti-patterns WARN, plus Official-Sources-Used content ERROR and SKILL.md↔gotchas.md duplication ERROR), and `standards/skill-content-contract.md` documents per-file depth minimums (2 complete examples with Scenario/Problem/Solution/Why/Source, 3 gotchas, pillar-specific WAF guidance) with a Block-commit severity table. The actual gap: that contract is explicitly scoped as "quality gates that scripts cannot check" (skill-content-contract.md:263), so nothing mechanically enforces it — `skills/flow/flow-interview-debugging` passes validate_repo.py with a 178-byte anti-patterns file of five bare noun phrases because five numbered lines satisfy a count. Fix is to promote the existing contract minimums into validators.py (e.g. per-example structural-heading check in examples.md, a chars-per-anti-pattern floor) and raise the <5 case from WARN to ERROR — not to invent a gate concept the repo lacks.

refuted_claims.lens: AGENT LAYER — 47 active runtime agents, 14 build-time, 14 deprecated aliases; contract compliance, skill-coverage diff, new-agent proposals, alias hygiene, inputs schemas, overlap
refuted_claims.title: suggest_agent misroutes 5 of 8 realistic vertical queries and has no abstain path — it always returns 3 confident picks
refuted_claims.reason:
The underlying structural observation is real but the claim as written is overstated and its evidence is not reproducible on HEAD.

WHAT IS TRUE (verified):
- /Users/pranavnagrecha/VS Code/Personal/SfSkills/mcp/sfskills-mcp/src/sfskills_mcp/routing.py line 16 does say "narrows the field from 47 candidates to 3".
- There is a DEFAULT_MIN_TREE_SCORE = 20.0 floor (line 150) for decision trees, but NO equivalent agent-score floor. `grep -rn "abstain|min_agent|no agent covers|request-skill" mcp/sfskills-mcp/src/` returns ZERO hits.
- `_INTENT_RULES` is 25 regex rules (grep -c re.compile = 25, one of which is _QUERY_TOKEN_RE, so 25 rules incl. the token regex) and contains no rule for omnistudio/omniscript/dataraptor/flexcard/field service/work order/CPQ/quote/pricing/commerce/marketing cloud/journey/CRM Analytics/Data Cloud.
- No agent exists for field service, CPQ, CRM Analytics, Data Cloud, commerce, or marketing (`ls agents/ | grep -i "field-service|cpq|analytics|data-cloud|commerce|marketing"` → empty), so those queries have no correct answer to return — which is the strongest form of the abstain argument.
- AGENT_CONTRACT.md:132 does contain the quoted rule 1.

WHY IT IS REFUTED AS STATED:
1. Evidence is stale / not reproducible. Their query 2 output omits `omnistudio-designer`. Re-running on HEAD, "design an OmniScript for insurance quoting" returns omnistudio-designer at #2 (score 35.0, tied with omni-channel-routing-designer). `agents/omnistudio-designer/AGENT.md` has `class: runtime`, `status: stable`. So the flagship "no omnistudio coverage" example is wrong — the agent exists and IS surfaced in the top 3. The same agent would also be the right answer for the Vlocity/DataRaptor query, making that a rule-coverage bug, not an abstain bug.
2. "it always returns 3 confident picks" is false on three counts: (a) their OWN evidence shows 2 results for the sharing query and 1 for the story query; (b) a genuinely unmatched query DOES abstain — `suggest_agent('xyzzy quantum blockchain sprocket')` returns `agents: []` and `next_step: ""`; (c) the payload emits no `confidence` field at all — `list(result.keys())` is `['task','agents','decision_trees','min_tree_score','next_step']`, and the docstring is explicit that "The caller's LLM still picks; this tool just narrows the field."
3. "misroutes 5 of 8" conflates two distinct defects — missing intent rules for verticals that DO have agents (omnistudio) and missing agents entirely (field service, CPQ, CRM Analytics). Only 2 of the 8 are true router failures with a reachable correct answer.
4. P0 is not defensible: this is a hint tool behind a mandatory `get_agent` follow-up, not an output surface; tests/test_routing.py already enforces top-1 ≥80% / top-3 ≥90% on a ≥20-case fixture, so the in-domain routing contract is gated. P2 (routing hygiene) is the honest severity.
refuted_claims.corrected: suggest_agent has no minimum AGENT score floor (only DEFAULT_MIN_TREE_SCORE=20.0 for decision trees), so when a broad verb rule like `\bdesign\b`/`\bbuild\b`/`\bmigrat` fires on an out-of-scope vertical query, it returns low-scoring, often tied garbage (e.g. "migrate our Vlocity DataRaptors" → automation-migration-router / bulk-migration-planner / profile-to-permset-migrator, all tied at 25.0) instead of signalling "no agent covers this — flag confidence: LOW and use /request-skill" per AGENT_CONTRACT.md:132. It DOES already abstain when nothing matches at all (`suggest_agent('xyzzy quantum blockchain sprocket')` → `agents: []`), and it emits no `confidence` field, so it is not "always 3 confident picks". Two separable fixes: (a) add a min_agent_score floor plus an explicit no-coverage next_step for tied/low-score results; (b) add _INTENT_RULES entries for omnistudio/omniscript/dataraptor/flexcard/vlocity → `omnistudio` (that agent exists and is runtime — it already reaches #2 on "OmniScript" but loses top-1 to omni-channel-routing-designer on a 35.0 tie). Field service, CPQ, CRM Analytics, Data Cloud, commerce and marketing have no agent at all, so those are roster-coverage gaps, not routing bugs. Severity P2, not P0.

refuted_claims.title: 20 of 47 active agents send users to deprecated agents; config-workbook-author hard-codes five of them and would then refuse its own output
refuted_claims.reason:
The underlying staleness is real but the claim is overstated on its two load-bearing points.

(1) COUNT IS WRONG. Re-running their command yields 18 active runtime agents naming deprecated agent ids, not 20. Their own pasted output was truncated mid-`story-drafter`, so they appear to have extrapolated. The full list is 18: agentforce-action-reviewer, business-hours-and-holidays-configurator, config-workbook-author, data-loader-pre-flight, data-model-reviewer, entitlement-and-milestone-designer, experience-cloud-admin-designer, fit-gap-analyzer, object-designer, omni-channel-routing-designer, path-designer, permission-set-architect, process-flow-mapper, profile-to-permset-migrator, sales-stage-designer, story-drafter, user-access-diff, waf-assessor. Adding legacy-slash-command-only references brings in exactly one more (security-scanner) = 19. `audit-router` also matches but legitimately owns all 14 aliases.

(2) THE HEADLINE SELF-CONTRADICTION IS FALSE. `config-workbook-author` would NOT refuse its own output. The operative test at line 246 and line 340 is "confirm the `recommended_agent` exists in `agents/_shared/RUNTIME_VS_BUILD.md`". RUNTIME_VS_BUILD.md line 96 has an explicit `### Deprecated (14)` section listing all fourteen — including `record-type-and-layout-auditor`, `validation-rule-auditor`, `sharing-audit-agent`, `lightning-record-page-auditor`, `report-and-dashboard-auditor` — with their aliases and `Superseded by: audit-router`. All five hard-coded values pass the existence check. The parenthetical "(typo, deprecated, freelanced)" is a gloss on why a value might be absent, not a second independent test. This is an ambiguous parenthetical, not a refuse-its-own-output contradiction. Also, lines 215-220 are prose section descriptions ("Recommend `X` for verification"), not literal `recommended_agent` field values in a plan schema.

(3) "SENDS USERS TO" OVERSTATES THE HARM. Every deprecated AGENT.md is a redirect stub (`status: deprecated`, `deprecated_in_favor_of: audit-router`, body = "route to /audit-router --domain sharing"), and the 9 legacy slash commands referenced by active agents all still exist in commands/ as forwarding aliases. docs/MIGRATION.md documents the whole contract and the Wave 7 removal window. Nobody hits a dead end today — they hit one extra hop.

WHAT IS GENUINELY TRUE AND WORTH FIXING: `pipelines/agent_validators.py` line 336-349 (`followup_agent` pattern `agents/([a-z0-9-]+)`) checks only that a referenced agent folder exists, never its status — and the pattern only matches path-form citations, so the bare-backtick prose references (`sharing-audit-agent`) that make up nearly all 18 hits are not linted at all. `standards/validation-gates.md` has exactly one deprecation-aware gate (line 74, cross-agent prose duplication). So there is no gate preventing this drift from growing. That is a P3 hygiene/lint gap, not a P1 routing failure.
refuted_claims.corrected: 18 active runtime agents (19 counting legacy-slash-command-only references) name Wave-3b deprecated agent ids or alias commands in prose without annotating them as superseded by `audit-router`, and `pipelines/agent_validators.py:336-349` only resolves that a follow-up agent folder exists — it never checks `status`, and its regex matches only `agents/<slug>` path form, so bare-backtick prose mentions are unlinted entirely. Fixing this means adding a status-aware follow-up gate plus a prose-form pattern, then annotating the 18 files. It is NOT true that `config-workbook-author` would refuse its own output: all 14 deprecated agents are explicitly listed in the `### Deprecated (14)` table of `agents/_shared/RUNTIME_VS_BUILD.md` (line 96), so the existence test at lines 246/340 passes. Nor do these references dead-end users — every deprecated AGENT.md is a redirect stub and all 9 referenced aliases still ship in commands/. Severity is P3 (documentation hygiene + missing lint), not P1.

refuted_claims.corrected: Real underlying gap, but the claim's headline and scope are both wrong. refuted_claims.title: Docs and the pre-push hook claim full validation takes 10–20s; measured runtime is ~11 minutes, and the fast-path flags are absent from the contributor-facing doc
refuted_claims.reason:
The claim is a bundle of three allegations; only the first survives, and the two that carry the "documentation gap" weight are false or misleading, so the P1 framing is overstated.

(1) VERIFIED, and worse than claimed: the "~10–20s" strings do exist in `.githooks/pre-push:20` and `AGENTS.md:46`, and my own timed run of shard 0/4 took 267s (not 170s), implying ~1068s (~17.8 min) for the sequential 4-shard loop the hook actually runs. `git config core.hooksPath` returns `.githooks`, so the hook is live. `CHANGELOG.md:294` shows where the number came from — "Full-repo validation time reduced from ~16 minutes to ~40 seconds across 4 CI shards" — i.e. the figure was always a *parallel CI matrix* number (`.github/workflows/validate.yml` fans out `shard: [0,1,2,3]`), copied into a hook that loops sequentially. So the true defect is a stale/miscopied number, not a missing document.

(2) REFUTED: "no doc explaining to a contributor that a generated-artifact ERROR is fixed by re-running sync." `CONTRIBUTING.md` "What Gets Rejected" table has the literal row `| Generated artifacts are stale | Re-run \`skill_sync.py --all\` |`, and the validator's own ERROR string already prints ``run `python3 scripts/skill_sync.py --all` ``. Both `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENT_RULES.md` also state the sync-then-validate order. This sub-claim is simply wrong.

(3) OVERSTATED: "AGENT_RULES.md ... which contributors are not told to read." `CONTRIBUTING.md:311` under "Getting Help" says `- Read authoring rules: \`AGENT_RULES.md\``, and Gate 2 already routes contributors to `standards/`. The fast-path flags (`--changed-only`, `--shard`, `--domain`) genuinely are not restated in CONTRIBUTING.md's body — that part is accurate — but they are documented in a table at `AGENT_RULES.md:104-108` that CONTRIBUTING.md explicitly links, so this is a cross-reference-depth nit, not an undocumented capability.

Net: one real, low-blast-radius stale string (a cosmetic ETA in a hook echo and one AGENTS.md bullet; the hook still works and prints its own bypass instructions), plus two invented gaps. Not P1.
refuted_claims.corrected: P3 (cosmetic doc drift): the "~10–20s" ETA in `.githooks/pre-push:20` and `AGENTS.md:46` is a stale Wave-1 figure that describes the *parallel* CI matrix (per CHANGELOG.md:294), not the *sequential* 4-shard loop the local hook runs. Measured today: 267s for shard 0/4 alone, so the local pre-push is ~15-18 minutes. Fix is to correct the two strings (and optionally cross-link `--changed-only`/`--shard`/`--domain` from CONTRIBUTING.md's Gate 1 rather than only from AGENT_RULES.md:104-108). The claim's other two elements are false: CONTRIBUTING.md's "What Gets Rejected" table already documents "Generated artifacts are stale → Re-run `skill_sync.py --all`", and CONTRIBUTING.md:311 does tell contributors to read AGENT_RULES.md.
