2. The exporter's epilog (`scripts/export_skills.py:963-971`) lists six examples and `--install` is not among them; the only filtered/unfiltered guidance there is `--domain apex`. The `--install` help text itself (`scripts/export_skills.py:1022-1029`) ends with "Combine with --domain/--skill to install a subset." So the exporter documents scoping at the exact point of use.
3. The documented install path in README:79-98 is: clone repo, pip install requirements, `search_knowledge.py`, and "Claude Code picks the repo up automatically via CLAUDE.md". The repo has no `.claude/skills/` directory (`ls -la .claude` → commands/, settings.local.json, workflows/, worktrees/ only). Using the library as documented preloads ZERO skill descriptions; retrieval is lexical via `scripts/search_knowledge.py`.
4. Curated-subset distribution already exists in three forms: (a) `scripts/export_agent_bundle.py --agent <x>` ships one agent plus only its dependency skills — I ran it for `user-access-diff` and got 89 files / 8 SKILL.md, not 1027; (b) the MCP server (`mcp/sfskills-mcp/src/sfskills_mcp/server.py`) exposes `search_skill`/`get_skill`/`suggest_agent` for lazy retrieval and is labelled "recommended for live use" in `docs/installing-single-agents.md`; (c) `--domain`/`--skill` filters on `--install` itself, with per-domain costs as low as omnistudio (34 skills, ~3.4K tokens).

The residual truth is narrow: there is no named "core" preset (e.g. `--preset core`) and `--install` with no filter does install all 1027. That is a docs/ergonomics nit, not a P0 distribution blocker, and it is reachable only by ignoring both the README's documented path and the flag's own help text.
refuted_claims.corrected: `scripts/export_skills.py --install <dir>` has no filter default, so an unfiltered run copies all 1027 skills (~134K tokens of name+description preload in Claude Code / Cursor). There is no named "core" preset and no context-cost warning printed by `--install`. However, this is NOT the documented install path: README:79-98 documents clone + CLAUDE.md + search_knowledge.py (zero preload — the repo ships no .claude/skills/), docs/installing-single-agents.md recommends the MCP server (lazy search_skill/get_skill) or `export_agent_bundle.py` (8 skills for user-access-diff, not 1027), and the `--install` help text already says "Combine with --domain/--skill to install a subset." Severity is P3 ergonomics (add a `--preset core` and a size warning), not P0.

refuted_claims.title: The Aider export produces a single 17.9 MB / ~4.5M-token CONVENTIONS.md that no model can read
refuted_claims.reason:
The byte count reproduces (17.87 MB), but both load-bearing claims about what is "missing" are false.

(1) "Any size ceiling or content-selection strategy" is NOT missing. `export_skills.py` accepts `--domain` and `--skill` filters that work for the aider target: `--target aider --domain apex` produces a 2.67 MB file from 158 skills instead of 17.9 MB from 1027. And `docs/multi-ai-parity.md:172` documents the exact failure mode the claim asserts is undocumented: "the whole file is provided on every Aider invocation. This works for small skill libraries but produces context-pressure on a 700+-skill library. Use with a narrow `--domain` filter when invoking export for Aider in a specific project." Aider is also explicitly tiered as a second-class, best-effort target in that same contract doc ("Cannot represent per-skill routing; skills compressed into one file").

(2) "README line 47 instructs users to run `aider --read exports/aider/CONVENTIONS.md`" is fabricated. README.md is 197 lines and contains ZERO occurrences of "aider" (grep -c = 0). The only `aider --read` instruction in the repo is `mcp/sfskills-mcp/docs/CONNECT.md:540`, sitting under the heading "### Aider (CLI fallback, no native MCP)" and prefaced with "Aider doesn't yet speak MCP. Best-effort fallback" — i.e. already framed as a degraded path, not a recommended install.

Residual, much smaller: `export_aider()` (scripts/export_skills.py:280-335) emits no runtime size warning the way `_mirror_commands` does for Windsurf's 12 KB cap, and the parity doc's "~10 MB" figure at line 169 is stale against the measured 17.9 MB. That is a P3 doc-freshness + missing-warning nit, not a P1 packaging break.
refuted_claims.corrected: The Aider export has no runtime size guard and no auto-updating size figure: `export_aider()` in scripts/export_skills.py writes the full concatenation with no warning at any threshold (unlike `_mirror_commands`, which warns on Windsurf's 12 KB per-workflow cap), and docs/multi-ai-parity.md:169 still states "~10 MB" against a measured 17.9 MB / ~4.5M tokens for 1027 skills. Content selection itself already exists (`--domain` / `--skill`, verified: `--target aider --domain apex` → 2.67 MB) and the context-pressure limitation is already documented at docs/multi-ai-parity.md:172 with the prescribed `--domain` mitigation. Severity P3 (stale number + missing advisory warning), not P1.

refuted_claims.title: No release or versioning discipline for the library itself — 0 releases, no version, all CHANGELOG headings say [Unreleased]
refuted_claims.reason: Their evidence reproduces verbatim, so the CHANGELOG/VERSION observations are true. But the framing "no release or versioning discipline, 0 releases, no version identity" collapses under two checks they did not run. First, `gh release list` returned empty only because it targets the current remote (AwesomeSalesforceSkills); `gh api repos/PranavNagrecha/SfSkills/releases` returns three published releases (mcp-v0.4.0, 0.4.1, 0.4.4), each with sfskills-data.tar.gz plus wheel and sdist assets, on what is now AwesomeSalesforceSkills-archive. A release cadence existed and broke at the repo migration; it was never absent. Second, the library is versioned — .github/workflows/publish-mcp.yml builds the whole corpus (registry, vector_index, agents, skills, templates, standards, commands) into the release bundle keyed to the mcp-v* tag, and registry/skills.json plus registry/export_manifest.json carry schema_version, skill_count, generated_from_hash and per-target/per-skill sha256 hashes as a content-addressed catalog identity. The one real downstream symptom (init 404) is already self-documented at docs/getting-started.md:170-181. What survives is CHANGELOG hygiene plus one missing re-tagged release on the new remote, which is not P1.
refuted_claims.corrected: CHANGELOG hygiene is stale and the release stream stalled at the repo rename — not an absence of release/versioning discipline. Real and verified: no VERSION file, all 6 CHANGELOG headings read `## [Unreleased]`, the newest documents v0.4.3 while PyPI/pyproject/__init__ ship 0.4.6, and no entry exists for 0.4.5 or 0.4.6. But three load-bearing parts of the claim are wrong or overstated: (1) "0 GitHub releases" is an artifact of the repo rename — three real releases exist (mcp-v0.4.0 2026-05-08, mcp-v0.4.1 2026-05-08, mcp-v0.4.4 2026-05-12), each carrying `sfskills-data.tar.gz` plus the wheel and sdist, on PranavNagrecha/SfSkills which now resolves to PranavNagrecha/AwesomeSalesforceSkills-archive; the current remote AwesomeSalesforceSkills inherited the four `mcp-v*` tags (git ls-remote confirms all four, including mcp-v0.4.6) but not the release objects. (2) The library does have a version identity and a release mechanism: `.github/workflows/publish-mcp.yml` fires on `mcp-v*` tags, builds the corpus bundle from registry + vector_index + agents + skills + templates + standards + commands, attaches it to the release and publishes the wheel — so the skill library ships versioned by the mcp-v* tag, which is why the tags are "MCP-scoped". (3) The corpus additionally carries content-addressed identity: registry/skills.json has schema_version=1, skill_count=1027, generated_from_hash=3285fea0..., and registry/export_manifest.json has schema_version, generated_at, and a per-target sha256 overall_hash plus a per-skill hash. The genuinely broken consequence — `sfskills-mcp-init` 404ing on releases/latest/download/sfskills-data.tar.gz — is already documented in the repo at docs/getting-started.md:170-181, and docs/release-plans/v0.4.4-post-launch.md exists. Correct severity is P2/P3 documentation-and-re-tag work: cut a release on the current remote for mcp-v0.4.6, and rewrite the `[Unreleased]` headings with dates plus 0.4.5/0.4.6 entries.

refuted_claims.title: A date stamp in a drift-checked generated file makes validate_repo.py fail every day on a clean tree — the repo has been red since 2026-07-09
refuted_claims.reason: Three independent findings refute the claim as stated. (1) The stated precondition is false — `git status --porcelain` returns 34 lines, not nothing; `docs/queue-progress.md` is itself locally modified and already re-stamped to 2026-07-31, so re-running their exact snippet in this tree prints `identical: True`, the opposite of their pasted output. (2) The "fires in every CI shard" mechanism does not hold: `validate.yml` runs `scripts/build_index.py` before `validate_repo.py`, and `build_index.py` calls `write_state`, which writes `docs/queue-progress.md` from the freshly-built state (`sync_engine.py:336-337`). The drift check therefore always compares a file the same job just regenerated. (3) The claim "the repo has been red since 2026-07-09" is directly contradicted by CI history: the most recent 12 `validate` runs are all `success`, and the decisive case is run 28988818999 (2026-07-09T02:01:47Z, UTC date 2026-07-09) validating commit 14f9b2490 whose committed dashboard reads `# Queue progress dashboard — 2026-07-08` — exactly the stale-by-a-day condition the claim says is fatal — reporting "0 error(s)" on shards 0-3. The underlying non-idempotency is real (a clean clone of HEAD shows a date-only diff, confirmed below) and worth a cheap fix, but it is a pre-push/manual-run annoyance with a one-command remedy, not a P0 red build.
refuted_claims.corrected: The date-stamp mechanism is real but the impact is misdiagnosed and the severity is overstated. `scripts/generate_queue_dashboard.py:279` / `pipelines/sync_engine.py:266-270` do render `date.today()` into `docs/queue-progress.md` (L1 heading, L7 "Last refresh"), and `sync_engine.diff_state()` (L387-388) does include that file, so a bare `python3 scripts/validate_repo.py` on a checkout whose dashboard was last regenerated on an earlier calendar day emits one ERROR whose only content delta is the date. But it does NOT make the build red: every consumer that matters regenerates the artifact first. CI's `validate.yml:43` runs `python3 scripts/build_index.py` (which calls `write_state`, and `sync_engine.py:336-337` writes `docs/queue-progress.md`) immediately before `validate_repo.py --skills-only --shard N/4` at line 54, so the workspace copy is re-stamped with the runner's date before the drift check reads it. `.githooks/pre-commit:9` likewise runs `skill_sync.py --changed-only` before `validate_repo.py --changed-only`. Empirically the repo is green, not red: the 12 most recent `validate` runs all succeeded, including run 28988818999 at 2026-07-09T02:01Z which validated a dashboard stamped `2026-07-08` (UTC day boundary already crossed) with "0 error(s)" on all four shards. The genuine residual exposure is narrow — `.githooks/pre-push:24` calls `validate_repo.py` with no preceding sync, so pushing on a later calendar day than the last commit/sync trips it — and the fix is the message the validator already prints (`skill_sync.py --all`). Severity is P3 non-idempotent-generated-artifact hygiene (drop `today` from the rendered text, or normalize it in `diff_state`), not P0. The claim's evidence is also partly fabricated: `git status --porcelain` is NOT empty in this working tree (34 entries: 21 modified files including `docs/queue-progress.md` itself, plus untracked `agents/omnistudio-designer/`, `docs/README.md` and others), so the asserted "tree is clean" precondition never held.

refuted_claims.title: The 1,356-fixture retrieval-quality gate — the check that protects the core product promise — runs in zero CI jobs and zero hooks
refuted_claims.reason:
The evidence command reproduces (with one line-number error: the pre-push hook match is `.githooks/pre-push:24`, not `:34`), and the CI/pre-push half of the claim is true: all four `validate.yml` shards and all four `pre-push` shards pass `--skip-fixture-retrieval`, and nothing in `.github/` or `.githooks/` invokes `evals/scripts/run_evals.py` or `evals/measurement/retrieval_eval.py`. But the headline is factually wrong on two counts, which is why this is refuted-as-overstated rather than accepted.

(1) "runs in zero CI jobs and ZERO HOOKS" and "only ever exercised when a human manually types a bare `python3 scripts/validate_repo.py`" are both false. `.githooks/pre-commit:13` runs `python3 scripts/validate_repo.py --changed-only` with NO skip flag, and `git config core.hooksPath` returns `.githooks`, so the hook is live in this working copy. Reading `scripts/validate_repo.py:355-374`, `--changed-only` narrows `fixtures_to_run` to fixtures whose `expected_skill` is in the touched set but still executes `build_search_context` + `run_search` and still emits the `did not return ... in top N` ERROR. The claim's own body concedes this and then contradicts its own title. So every commit that adds or edits a skill IS automatically retrieval-gated for that skill — which is the single highest-risk moment (a newly authored skill that its own query can't retrieve is blocked at commit).

(2) I proved the non-skipped path is live and catches real failures by running a domain-scoped validation: `--domain omnistudio` (34 skills, 40 fixtures) ran the retrieval gate and produced `ERROR ... query 'translate omniscript' did not return 'omnistudio/omnistudio-multi-language' in top 3`. That same ERROR would fire from the pre-commit hook if that skill were touched.

(3) The gap is also already documented in-repo, not undiscovered: `docs/comparison.md:107-112` states verbatim "The quality gates that would prove all of this are switched off ... `--skip-fixture-retrieval`, so the retrieval-quality gate does not run in CI."

What IS real: the FULL-CORPUS sweep never runs automatically. Nothing catches cross-skill regressions — skill A's enrichment pushing skill B's fixture out of top-3 — because `--changed-only` only re-runs B's fixture if B itself was touched. Given the known zero-sum 30-chunk lexical window, that is a genuine hole, and the Wave-6 re-enable note at `validate.yml:45-52` is stale (Wave 6 shipped; the export-parity matrix in the same file is labelled Wave 6). But it is a partial-coverage hole, not "the gate never runs" — severity is P1/P2, not P0. Also confirmed the incidental sub-claims: the full run is slow (34 skills alone took 3m32s wall, so ~12m for 1,356 fixtures is credible) and it currently exits 1 for unrelated doc-count drift (`agents_total is 75 in doc but canonical is 76`, `active_runtime is 47 ... canonical is 48`).
refuted_claims.corrected: The full-corpus retrieval-quality sweep (1,356 fixtures) runs in zero CI jobs and zero pre-push shards — all four `validate.yml` shards (`.github/workflows/validate.yml:54`) and all four `.githooks/pre-push:24` shards pass `--skip-fixture-retrieval`, and no workflow runs `evals/scripts/run_evals.py` or `evals/measurement/retrieval_eval.py`. It is NOT true that the gate never runs automatically: `.githooks/pre-commit:13` runs `validate_repo.py --changed-only` with retrieval ENABLED, so any skill you add or edit has its own fixtures asserted at commit time (verified: a scoped run emitted `ERROR ... query 'translate omniscript' did not return 'omnistudio/omnistudio-multi-language' in top 3`). The actual uncovered class is CROSS-SKILL retrieval regression — editing skill A can demote skill B's fixture out of top-3 and nothing automated re-checks B, because `--changed-only` filters fixtures to the touched skill set. Secondary: the `validate.yml:45-52` comment promising re-enablement "in Wave 6" is stale (Wave 6 shipped in the same file). The finding is already written up at `docs/comparison.md:107-112`. Severity P1/P2, not P0.

refuted_claims.title: CONTRIBUTING.md has not been touched since the initial 77-skill commit and omits every gate added since — a human following it end-to-end hits undocumented hard ERRORs
refuted_claims.reason:
The factual half is real — CONTRIBUTING.md's only commit is 70fb00955 (2026-04-03, initial 77-skill commit), and it genuinely omits `architect` from its domain-folder list (skills/architect/ exists), never mentions `audit_duplicates.py`, `--strict`, `--agent`, or `llm-anti-patterns.md`, and points at MASTER_QUEUE.md 4 times. But the claimed *mechanism* and P0 severity are wrong, so the claim as written is overstated.

(1) The headline "a human following it end-to-end hits undocumented hard ERRORs" is false for the flagship gate they cite. validate_repo.py:449 (runtime_orphan ERROR) is unreachable by a human following CONTRIBUTING Step 4 verbatim: `scripts/new_skill.py:792-805` makes the agent-wiring decision mandatory *at scaffold time* — in a TTY it drops into `_prompt_agent_decision()`, and in non-TTY it hard-exits with a message naming both `--agent` and `--runtime-orphan`. So the flags CONTRIBUTING omits are self-documenting at the point of use. And in the residual case where the ERROR did fire, validate_repo.py:450-457 prints the exact remediation command (`patch_agent_skill.py <agent_id> <skill_id> ...`) plus the `runtime_orphan: true` alternative — i.e. the gate documents itself. Nothing here is "undocumented."

(2) The `references/llm-anti-patterns.md` ERROR (pipelines/validators.py:263) likewise cannot bite a scaffold-following contributor: `new_skill.py:829` writes the file automatically, and CONTRIBUTING Step 4 already says "Fill every marker — do not leave any," which covers the TODO-marker ERROR. The only genuinely undocumented sub-gate is the 5-anti-pattern minimum.

(3) MASTER_QUEUE.md still exists at repo root and its own first lines redirect to BACKLOG.yaml, so the stale pointer self-corrects on arrival rather than dead-ending.

(4) The staleness is not unique to CONTRIBUTING and is arguably worse in the doc the claim treats as the source of truth: AGENT_RULES.md:132 still says validate_repo "emits a WARN for skills cited by no agent. The WARN is a flag, not a gate" — directly contradicting the ERROR at validate_repo.py:449. A gap statement that frames CONTRIBUTING as uniquely frozen while the canonical rules file carries a contradictory description of the same gate is mis-scoped.

What survives is a genuine but low-severity doc-freshness defect: five stale/missing items in a contributor-facing doc, none of which block a merge or produce an unexplained failure. That is P2/P3 documentation drift, not a P0.
refuted_claims.corrected: CONTRIBUTING.md has not been updated since the initial commit (70fb00955, 2026-04-03) and has drifted from the current workflow: its domain-folder list omits `architect` (a real skills/ folder with a category/folder-match gate), it never mentions `scripts/audit_duplicates.py` or `--strict` (steps 2 and 4 of CLAUDE.md's required workflow), its Step 5 "Fill the package" file-minimums list omits `references/llm-anti-patterns.md` and its 5-anti-pattern minimum (pipelines/validators.py:263-275), and it references `MASTER_QUEUE.md` 4 times although row data moved to `BACKLOG.yaml` on 2026-05-01. It does NOT cause contributors to hit undocumented hard ERRORs: the agent-wiring decision is enforced interactively at scaffold time by `new_skill.py:792-805` (TTY prompt) or by a hard exit naming both flags (non-TTY), `llm-anti-patterns.md` is auto-scaffolded at `new_skill.py:829`, and the validate_repo.py:449 ERROR prints its own `patch_agent_skill.py` remediation command. Severity: P2/P3 doc drift. Note the same drift exists in AGENT_RULES.md:132, which still describes the agent-citation gate as a WARN rather than the ERROR it is.

refuted_claims.title: 16,866 lines of scripts/ + pipelines/ have zero unit tests; the only harness tests skill checkers and is not in CI
refuted_claims.reason: Re-running the evidence command reproduces the root-config nulls (no pytest.ini/tox.ini/conftest.py/pyproject.toml at repo root) and I independently confirmed the hard core of the gap: `grep -rln 'import unittest\|import pytest' scripts/ pipelines/` returns nothing (exit=1), and no test file anywhere imports pipelines.validators, pipelines.sync_engine, pipelines.similarity or pipelines.chunker. So "no unit tests for the drift oracle and the ~30 gates" is real and I would not dismiss it. But the claim's headline and two of its four supporting bullets are false or materially misleading. (a) "the only harness tests skill checkers and is not in CI": there are 24 test files / 3,923 lines under mcp/sfskills-mcp/tests with a pyproject.toml, and CI runs three of them — validate.yml:85 and pr-lint.yml:32 run tests.test_agent_frontmatter, validate.yml:95 runs tests.test_tools, validate.yml:131 and pr-lint.yml:66 run tests.test_export_parity. The claimant's own evidence command never looked for tests outside the root and mcp/sfskills-mcp/tests/*.py greps, so it missed the CI wiring entirely. (b) "test_checkers is referenced by no workflow and no hook" — literally true, but it IS invoked as a gate by scripts/ship_skills.py:66, which the claimant's grep (restricted to .github/ and .githooks/) could not see; calling it an orphan harness is wrong. (c) "The MCP suite does not import pipelines at all (one hit, a comment)" — no test imports it directly, but mcp/sfskills-mcp/src/sfskills_mcp/skills.py:184-186 imports pipelines.lexical_index, pipelines.ranking and pipelines.embedding_backends, and tests/test_skills.py:23 imports that module and calls search_skill against the real index, so lexical_index/ranking do get smoke coverage (uncredited by the claim, though correctly not in CI). (d) There is additionally a CI job the claim ignores — bench-orchestration in validate.yml:140-158 runs scripts/validate_repo_bench.py over a synthetic 500-skill corpus with a 30s threshold, gated on PRs touching the validator or pipelines/. That is a perf gate, not a correctness gate, but it is a CI harness pointed at the validator. (e) Minor: LOC is 17,019 today, not 16,866. Marking refuted because the claim as written overstates — the residual, correctly-scoped gap is narrower than "16,866 lines have zero tests and the only harness isn't in CI".
refuted_claims.corrected: The core defect holds but the framing is wrong on two counts. Accurate version: "pipelines/ (13 modules incl. validators.py, sync_engine.py, similarity.py, ranking.py, lexical_index.py, chunker.py) and the 44 scripts/ entrypoints have no direct unit tests — no file in scripts/ or pipelines/ imports unittest or pytest, and no test anywhere imports pipelines.validators, sync_engine, similarity or chunker. Their only coverage is (a) running validate_repo.py / skill_sync.py over the real corpus in .githooks/pre-commit, .githooks/pre-push and the 4-shard validate.yml job, (b) a perf-only bench (scripts/validate_repo_bench.py, 500 synthetic skills, threshold 30s) in the bench-orchestration CI job, and (c) smoke-level transitive exercise of lexical_index/ranking/sync_engine via mcp/sfskills-mcp/tests/test_skills.py, which is itself not run in CI. Behavioural gates are therefore asserted only against the live corpus, so a validator that silently stops firing cannot be caught." What is NOT true: (1) "the only harness tests skill checkers" — there is a 24-file, 3,923-line unittest suite at mcp/sfskills-mcp/tests/, with its own pyproject.toml; (2) "and is not in CI" — three of those suites (test_agent_frontmatter, test_tools, test_export_parity) run in .github/workflows/validate.yml and pr-lint.yml on every PR; (3) "test_checkers.py ... is not referenced by any workflow or hook" is true literally but misleading — it is a gate inside scripts/ship_skills.py:66 (`test_checkers (changed)`), the repo's ship pipeline. Also the LOC figure has drifted: 17,019, not 16,866.

refuted_claims.title: The bench that is supposed to guard validator cost passes with 14x slack while the real path is 60x slower per skill
refuted_claims.reason:
The factual skeleton reproduces, but the framing ("fake guard", P1) and every quantitative figure are wrong or unstable.

1. NOTHING IS HIDDEN. The claim's core rhetorical move — that the bench secretly excludes the expensive paths — is contradicted by the bench's own docstring, which the claimant even quotes from. scripts/validate_repo_bench.py:1-22 states in plain text: "The bench only measures orchestration throughput", plus a named paragraph justifying each skip ("Why --skip-drift:", "Why --skip-fixture-retrieval: ... retrieval quality is already tested by the real-repo validation run"), and _run_bench's docstring (lines ~140-160) explains --skip-similarity and adds "Correctness of those rules is tested by the real-repo validation run — this bench only measures orchestration throughput." A guard that documents its own scope in its module docstring is a scoped guard, not a fake one. It never claims to defend total validator wall-clock.

2. "14x headroom" is not a stable number. Across five runs on this machine I measured 14.19s, 9.71s, 4.01s, 3.53s, 2.94s (threshold 30s) — headroom ranges 2.1x to 10.2x depending on machine load, not a fixed 14x. The derived assertion "a change could make the orchestrator 10x slower and still pass" holds only on an idle machine.

3. "60x slower per skill" is fabricated arithmetic. Their own numbers give 130s/263 = 0.494 s/skill real vs 2.16s/500 = 0.0043 s/skill bench = 114x, not 60x. Mine give 258s/263 = 0.98 vs 0.0059-0.028 = 35x-166x. No run produces 60x.

4. Real-path timing is machine-dependent, not "130s". My shard-0/4 run took 4:18.59 (258s) wall under concurrent load, and the run errored differently (27 errors, 6 warnings vs their "1 error, 9 warnings") — the repo state they benchmarked is not reproducible either.

5. Line citation wrong: the pre-push echo is .githooks/pre-push:20, not :29.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE AND SMALL: (a) the two timing comments are stale by an order of magnitude — validate.yml:3-4 "686+ skills ... ~40 seconds wall-clock" and pre-push:20 "~10–20s" for 4 sequential shards; (b) the bench docstring overclaims by listing "script --help fan-out" among what it measures, when _seed_skill() creates an empty scripts/ dir so zero of the real corpus's 1057 skill-local .py files are exercised. Both are doc-accuracy fixes (P3), not a P1 broken guard.
refuted_claims.corrected: Two timing comments are stale by an order of magnitude, and the bench docstring overclaims one line of coverage. (P3, doc accuracy.) `.github/workflows/validate.yml:3-4` says "686+ skills validate in ~40 seconds wall-clock" and `.githooks/pre-push:20` says "4 shards, ~10–20s", while one shard of 263 skills now takes minutes (130s-258s measured), making the 4-shard sequential pre-push several minutes. Separately, `scripts/validate_repo_bench.py`'s module docstring lists "script `--help` fan-out" among what the bench measures, but `_seed_skill()` creates an empty `scripts/` dir, so none of the real corpus's 1057 skill-local `.py --help` subprocesses — the dominant cost — are exercised; that clause should be removed. The bench itself is not defective: it explicitly and repeatedly documents that it measures orchestration throughput only, and defers correctness, similarity, and retrieval to the real-repo run. Its 30s threshold has roughly 2x-10x headroom depending on machine load (measured 2.94s-14.19s), not a fixed 14x.

refuted_claims.title: 11,405 fenced code blocks in skills/ are never syntax-checked; 79 of 290 JSON blocks do not parse
refuted_claims.reason: Two-part verdict. (1) The structural claim survives: I reproduced `grep -cniE 'code_block|fenced|javascript' pipelines/validators.py` = 0, and searching scripts/, pipelines/, .github/workflows/, and all 1,057 skill-local checkers found no code-block content validation anywhere — every fence reference in the codebase is fence-*skipping* logic. (2) The severity claim collapses under inspection. I independently reproduced the exact counts (290/79 JSON, 147/14 YAML) with my own parser, then classified the failures: 70/79 invalid JSON blocks are property-level fragments of larger files (do not start with `{` or `[`), and all 9 whole-document failures carry explicit elision markers (`[...]`, `{ ... }`, `/* ... */`) or are annotated wrong/right pairs. Reading the three specific locations the claim cites as samples (scratch-org-management/references/gotchas.md:30, unlocked-package-development/SKILL.md:133) shows both are deliberate teaching devices, not truncation or malformation. The apex brace hits are likewise one-line signature excerpts under `// WRONG` / `**Correct pattern:**` headers. The claim's framing — "57 remain unparseable after comment-stripping (multiple documents in one fence, elisions, truncation)" presented as a P1 quality defect that would break a practitioner's paste — misreads standard documentation convention as corpus rot. Refuted as overstated, not as already-satisfied.
refuted_claims.corrected: No validator inspects fenced-code-block *contents* — that structural fact is confirmed (`grep -cniE 'code_block|fenced|javascript' pipelines/validators.py` = 0; the only fence handling in `pipelines/validators.py` (lines 275, 387-394, 441-450, 500-530) and `pipelines/agent_validators.py:513` *strips/skips* fences so prose gates don't false-positive on them; `.github/workflows/validate.yml` has no markdown or code lint step; none of the 1,057 skill-local `check_*.py` scripts parse the skill's own fences). But the claimed evidence of harm is wrong. The raw counts reproduce exactly (json: 290 blocks / 79 invalid; yaml: 147 / 14; apex decl blocks with unbalanced braces: 10-14 depending on comment/string stripping), yet the failures are almost entirely *intentional documentation fragments*, not defects: 70 of the 79 "invalid" JSON blocks do not even begin with `{` or `[` — they are excerpts of a larger file keyed at the property level (e.g. `"dependencies": [ {...} ]` in skills/devops/unlocked-package-development/SKILL.md:133, `"datasets": [...]` in skills/admin/analytics-dashboard-json/references/llm-anti-patterns.md:10). Only 9 begin as whole documents, and every one of those is an API-response illustration with an explicit elision marker (`"records": [...]`, `"Data": { ... }`, `[ /* up to batchSize records */ ]`) or a deliberate WRONG-vs-CORRECT pair annotated with `//` inside one fence (skills/devops/scratch-org-management/references/gotchas.md:30 — the cited "practitioner pastes it into project-scratch-def.json" scenario is a labelled `// Old (deprecated)` / `// New (correct)` migration example, not something anyone would paste whole). The apex hits are the same pattern: all sampled ones are one-line signature snippets by design (`trigger AccountChangeEventTrigger on AccountChangeEvent (before insert) {` under a `// WRONG` header). A naive `json.loads` / brace-balance gate would therefore fire on ~79 blocks of which ~0 are actual bugs — a false-positive rate near 100%. This is at most a P3 "nice-to-have lint, gated on an explicit opt-in fence marker for complete-document blocks", not a P1 corpus-quality defect.

refuted_claims.title: min_skill_score=1.5 is arithmetically unreachable for single-chunk matches, so correct answers are reported as "no coverage"
refuted_claims.reason:
The claim describes a single-threshold gate that does not exist in the code. `scripts/search_knowledge.py:256` gates on an OR, not on `min_skill_score` alone:

    if s["max_score"] >= ctx.min_skill_max_score or s["score"] >= ctx.min_skill_score

and `config/retrieval-config.yaml:62` sets `min_skill_max_score: 1.0` right beside `min_skill_score: 1.5`. A skill matching exactly one chunk at position 0 scores 1.0 + 0.1 = 1.1 max_score, which clears the 1.0 arm. Single-chunk matches are therefore explicitly admitted — the exact scenario the claim says is arithmetically impossible.

Their evidence is self-refuting: their own diag output lists `admin/opportunity-management cum=1.239 max=1.239` as "DROP", but 1.239 >= 1.0, so the real gate keeps it. The diag script (`scratchpad/diag.py`) does not exist in the repo and evidently hardcoded a 1.5-only filter rather than calling `run_search`. Running the claim's own query through the real CLI returns `has_coverage = True` with that skill kept.

The config even documents this as a deliberate, swept fix for precisely the failure mode the claim reports ("Gating on `score` alone rewards breadth of weak matches and suppresses one precise match"): `score >= 1.5` alone gave fixture false-NONE 3 / held-out NONE 23.3%; the OR form gives false-NONE 0 / held-out NONE 6.7%. Also, `ceiling ≤ 1.3` ignores that `aggregate_skill_scores` adds a name/description centrality bonus (`rank_score`), though that is correctly excluded from the gate by design.

Caveat noted for honesty: `config/retrieval-config.yaml` and the search script changes are in the working tree (uncommitted, dated 2026-07-31), not yet in HEAD. The behavior is live in the checkout the analyst was measuring, so the claim is refuted against the repo as it stands.
refuted_claims.corrected: Not a gap. The coverage gate is `max_score >= 1.0 OR score >= 1.5`, so a single-chunk top-ranked match (1.1) passes. The only residual, non-P0 observation: the OR-gate + centrality-bonus retrieval work is currently uncommitted in the working tree and should be committed so it is not lost.

refuted_claims.title: The published 98.6% Hit@1 is measured with the answer's own domain supplied as a filter, on author-written trigger phrases; real natural-language Hit@1 is 36.1%
refuted_claims.reason:
Three of the claim's four load-bearing assertions are false; the mechanism is real but its magnitude is overstated by ~20x.

(1) MECHANISM — TRUE. `evals/measurement/retrieval_eval.py:119` does call `_search(query, domain=fx.get("domain"))`, and `pipelines/lexical_index.py:108-110` turns that into a hard `AND domain = ?` SQL filter, plus a redundant `+0.2` boost at `pipelines/ranking.py:88-90`. That part checks out.

(2) MAGNITUDE — FALSE, by ~20x. I ran my own A/B over a seeded 250-query sample of `vector_index/query-fixtures.json`, identical code path, only `domain` toggled: 98.4% Hit@1 with the hint vs 95.6% without — a 2.8pp leak, Hit@3 100.0% either way, coverage 100.0% either way. The claimant's OWN pasted evidence shows the same thing (97.0% -> 94.8%, 2.2pp). Their headline number "real natural-language Hit@1 is 36.1%" is not the domain-filter delta at all; it comes from an unshown, self-authored, self-graded 36-query set that they neither committed nor described, and it is contradicted by their own A/B in the same paragraph. The title asserts a causal link ("measured with the answer's own domain supplied ... real NL Hit@1 is 36.1%") that their own data refutes.

(3) "There is no independent, realistically-phrased skill-level eval set anywhere in the repo ... realistic_queries.json (71 entries) targets AGENT routing, not skills — every entry has corpus: agents" — FALSE, and trivially checkable. The committed file is 31 agents / 23 skills / 10 decision-trees / 7 templates. The 23 `corpus: "skills"` entries are exactly the artifact the claim says does not exist: hand-written realistic phrasings ("how do I write an apex test class", "how do I retry a failed apex callout") with verified skill labels and NO domain key. Its runner `evals/measurement/run_realistic_smoke.py:54` calls `search_knowledge.run_search(query, _skills_ctx())` — no domain argument, i.e. the real-user path. I ran those 23 domain-free: Hit@1 73.9% / Hit@3 91.3% / coverage 100.0%. (There is additionally an untracked `run_heldout.py` + `heldout-queries.json`, 154 hand-written domain-free queries with `--use-domain` OFF by default and a docstring stating "the published held-out numbers are domain-free" — I did not count it since it is uncommitted.)

(4) "The published 98.6%" as a bare, unqualified headline — FALSE. `mcp/sfskills-mcp/README.md:54-67` prints 98.6% inside a six-row table that also publishes Synthetic NL skills 74.5%, Realistic-user smoke 81.7%, Agents NL 95.5%, Templates NL 88.7%, Decision-trees NL 82.4%, followed by prose that explicitly disclaims the curated number: "The realistic-user smoke — hand-crafted queries with unambiguous expected answers — better reflects real-world quality at 81.7% Hit@1 / 94.4% Hit@3." The root `README.md` does not publish 98.6% at all (grep returns nothing). The curated row is labeled "Author-curated triggers (1,285 Q)" — the provenance the claim says is hidden is in the row label.

Also minor: "No CLI or MCP user ever passes --domain" is asserted, not shown, and both surfaces expose it (`scripts/search_knowledge.py:340` `--domain`, `mcp/.../server.py:167` `search_skill(query, domain=None, limit=10)`), so an agent caller that knows the category does pass it.

Net: a genuine but small methodological wart (a ~3pp domain hint in one harness, on trigger-derived fixtures) inflated into a P0 "the headline is 98.6% but reality is 36.1%" story, with the repo's existing domain-free skills smoke and its published NL table both overlooked. Severity is P3 hygiene, not P0.
refuted_claims.corrected: `evals/measurement/retrieval_eval.py:119` passes each fixture's own `domain` into `run_search`, which becomes a hard `AND domain = ?` SQL filter (`pipelines/lexical_index.py:108`) plus a `+0.2` rank boost (`pipelines/ranking.py:88`). This inflates the curated-fixture Hit@1 by roughly 3 percentage points (measured: 98.4% with the hint vs 95.6% without, on a 250-query sample; Hit@3 and coverage are unchanged at 100%). The fixtures are also paraphrases of the skills' own `triggers:` frontmatter, so they measure the easy case. Neither issue is hidden or unmeasured: `mcp/sfskills-mcp/README.md` publishes the curated number labeled "Author-curated triggers" alongside domain-free NL results (synthetic 74.5%, realistic smoke 81.7%) and states in prose that the realistic smoke better reflects real-world quality; `evals/measurement/run_realistic_smoke.py` runs 23 hand-written `corpus: "skills"` queries with no domain argument (measured 73.9% Hit@1 / 91.3% Hit@3 / 100% coverage). The remaining work is small and hygienic: default `retrieval_eval.py` to `domain=None` (or report both columns), and grow the 23-query domain-free skills smoke toward the ~150-query, per-category coverage the untracked `run_heldout.py` prototype already sketches. There is no 98.6%-vs-36.1% discrepancy; that figure is unreproducible from any committed fixture set and is contradicted by the claim's own A/B output.

refuted_claims.title: The retrieval-quality gate is switched off in CI and in the pre-push hook behind a stale "Wave 6" promise that is tracked nowhere
refuted_claims.reason:
The mechanical half of the claim reproduces (the flag is in validate.yml's 4-shard step and in .githooks/pre-push, and the "Wave 6 / Wave 4" comment is stale), but the two load-bearing conclusions are wrong.

(1) "All 1356 fixtures are dead weight — nothing verifies retrieval on any PR" is false. `.githooks/pre-commit` line 13 runs `python3 scripts/validate_repo.py --changed-only` with NO skip flag. In scripts/validate_repo.py the gate is `if fixtures_to_run and not skip_fixture_retrieval:` (line 367) and `fixtures_to_run` is filtered to `seen_ids` — i.e. the changed skills. So the retrieval-quality assertion runs locally on every commit for exactly the skills being touched, which is the regression surface a PR introduces. CLAUDE.md's mandated post-skill workflow also runs bare `python3 scripts/validate_repo.py` (gate on). Separately, the fixture *coverage* gate ("every skill must have a fixture") is unaffected by the flag and still runs in all four CI shards — documented at AGENT_RULES.md:108.

(2) "Tracked nowhere / grep finds no BACKLOG.yaml or docs/ entry" is false as stated: their own evidence command used a broken pattern (unescaped alternation inside a basic-regex grep, so `fixture-retrieval|retrieval gate|retrieval-quality` was matched literally). Re-run with `-E` and docs/comparison.md:107-110 explicitly documents the disabled gate as a known weakness. BACKLOG.yaml is a *skill* queue (925+ skill rows), not an engineering tracker — absence there is expected, not evidence of neglect.

(3) Severity P0 is inflated. CHANGELOG.md:188 records the curated 1,285-query fixture corpus at Hit@1 98.6% / Hit@3 100.0% as of 2026-05-09, and the gate's default top_k is 3 — so the stated justification ("~40 shallow skills return their expected skill outside top-3") is factually obsolete, and re-enabling would most likely pass rather than expose 40 failures. The real, smaller issue is a stale comment plus a dangling pointer: the comment says "See docs/multi-ai-parity.md (Wave 6) for the re-enable criteria" but that file contains no retrieval or re-enable content (only two "Wave 6" hits, neither about retrieval).

Note the flag is not merely cosmetic in CI: with embeddings enabled (config/retrieval-config.yaml `enabled: true`, fastembed, ~500 MB embeddings.jsonl) building the search context is expensive — my `--domain omnistudio` run with the gate on did not finish in 600s locally, which is a real cost argument for the CI skip that the claim never weighs.
refuted_claims.corrected: The retrieval-quality gate is skipped in the 4 CI shards and in pre-push, and its inline justification is stale (it cites "Wave 6 / Wave 4" and "~40 shallow skills outside top-3" when the curated 1,285-Q corpus has measured Hit@3 = 100.0% since 2026-05-09, and it points at docs/multi-ai-parity.md for re-enable criteria that file does not contain). It is NOT true that retrieval is unverified: .githooks/pre-commit runs `validate_repo.py --changed-only` with the gate ON for every touched skill, the fixture-coverage gate runs in all CI shards, and docs/comparison.md:107-110 already documents the CI skip as a known weakness. Correct severity is P2/P3 — a stale comment and a dangling doc pointer, plus a missing full-corpus regression net in CI (whose real blocker is cost: fastembed context build, not ~40 failing skills).

refuted_claims.title: Embeddings are enabled, cost 8.3s and 2.85GB per process, contribute exactly 0.0pp, and the shipped MCP server never uses them
refuted_claims.reason:
The claim's load-bearing assertions are false at HEAD.

(1) The code citation is fabricated/stale. `mcp/.../skills.py:113` is `def _registry_by_id()`, not a rerank call. The only `rerank_results` call in that file is at line 216 and reads `rerank_results(query_vector, lexical_rows, {}, domain, skill_embeddings=skill_embeddings)` — a real query vector (fastembed, gated on skill vectors existing) plus skill-level vectors. `grep -rn "rerank_results(None" mcp/ scripts/ pipelines/` returns nothing; `git log -S` shows that form last existed in commit 7be85c291, i.e. the claim quotes an old revision.

(2) "The shipped MCP never uses embeddings / is pure lexical regardless of config" is therefore wrong. It is a deliberate, documented design: `_skill_embeddings()` loads the 5 MB skill-vector file and its docstring explicitly says it "Deliberately NEVER loads vector_index/embeddings.jsonl (535 MB of chunk-level vectors)... the chunk file would cost half a gigabyte of RSS to change nothing." The MCP is doing exactly the thing the claim demands. The "8.3 s / 2.85 GB per process" cost does not apply to the MCP at all.

(3) "Contribute exactly 0.0pp" is a re-measurement of an already-documented null result, presented as new. `config/retrieval-config.yaml` records the 2026-05-09 benchmark: curated 98.6% → 98.6% (no lift, expected), and the natural-language audit 74.3%/86.0% → 74.5%/87.8% (+1.8pp Hit@3), with a documented weight sweep (0.35 regressed −4pp, 0.10 no lift, 0.2 chosen). The claim measured only curated fixtures and 36 realistic queries — precisely the two slices the config already says show no movement — and omits the NL slice where the lift was claimed.

(4) The evidence is not reproducible: `scratchpad/embdelta.py` does not exist in the repo (`ls scratchpad` → No such file or directory).

(5) "Gitignored so a fresh clone has none anyway" is not a defect — it is the stated design (`.gitignore:34-44` documents why, and `.githooks/pre-commit` passes `--skip-embeddings`). A missing file degrades cleanly to lexical (`rerank_results` docstring: "Either, both, or neither can be present").

Peak RSS also did not reproduce as stated (1.44 GB for embeddings.jsonl alone, not 2.85 GB).
refuted_claims.corrected: Narrow, real residual only: `scripts/search_knowledge.py:181` eagerly loads the 535 MB chunk-level `vector_index/embeddings.jsonl` (measured 8.75 s, ~1.4 GB RSS) into `SearchContext`, even though `pipelines/ranking.rerank_results` prefers the skill-level vector whenever `row["skill_id"]` is in `skill_embeddings` — and skill vectors cover 96.2% of retrieved chunk rows (229/6000 fallbacks over 200 fixtures). So the CLI pays a multi-second, gigabyte-scale load for a vector source that is consulted on <4% of rows. The fix is to make chunk-embedding loading opt-in in `search_knowledge.py` (as the MCP already does), NOT to disable embeddings. Secondary real nit: `vector_index/skill_embeddings.jsonl` is stale — 994 vectors vs 1027 registry skills.

refuted_claims.title: The mandated search command takes 24 seconds per invocation, making the documented workflow impractical
refuted_claims.reason:
Two of the three load-bearing assertions fail.

(1) "24.10s per invocation" is not a reproducible property. I ran the exact command three times on the same machine and got real 137.78s, 34.29s, and 93.78s — with user+sys only ~11-16s in every run. The wall time is dominated by page-cache state while streaming a 535 MB embeddings.jsonl + 126 MB chunks.jsonl, so it swings 4x run-to-run. "24.10s" is one lucky warm-cache sample presented as a constant; the real range is worse AND less stable, which means the number cannot carry a severity argument.

(2) "There is no daemon, no cache, no --fast mode" is flatly false. The repo ships a long-lived MCP server at mcp/sfskills-mcp/ whose search_skill tool is the runtime-agent retrieval surface. It reads vector_index/lexical.sqlite via FTS5 and reuses pipelines/ranking.py, and its own PKG-INFO states results "match scripts/search_knowledge.py exactly." Its loaders are @lru_cache(maxsize=1), and skills.py:73-82 carries an explicit comment: "Deliberately NEVER loads vector_index/embeddings.jsonl (535 MB of chunk-level vectors) ... the chunk file would cost half a gigabyte of RSS to change nothing." Measured: 2.94s for the first query in the process, 0.030s/query thereafter. That is precisely the daemon-plus-cache the claim says does not exist, and it was built deliberately with the stated rationale.

The same in-process reuse also already exists on the build side: SearchContext's docstring documents that build-once/reuse takes a 744-fixture run from ~16 minutes to ~15 seconds, and scripts/validate_repo.py:57 imports build_search_context/run_search to do exactly that.

What survives: the one-shot CLI genuinely does pay a cold load per process, and the sub-claim that chunks.jsonl is loaded in full only to resolve official sources is correct — ctx.chunks is referenced exactly once, at search_knowledge.py:259 in collect_official_sources, and nowhere else. That is a real, narrow optimization opportunity (P3 ergonomics). But the framing — a fixed 24s tax, no mitigation anywhere in the repo, documented workflow "impractical" — is refuted. Also note embeddings.jsonl, chunks.jsonl, skill_embeddings.jsonl and lexical.sqlite are all gitignored (.gitignore:7-44, confirmed by git ls-files showing only manifest.json / query-fixtures.json / query-variants.json tracked), so the 8.27s embeddings load is a locally-built-artifact cost, not something every clone inherits.
refuted_claims.corrected: scripts/search_knowledge.py has no per-process caching, so each one-shot CLI invocation re-streams the gitignored vector_index/embeddings.jsonl (535 MB) and chunks.jsonl (126 MB); wall time is page-cache-dependent and ranged 34-138s across three runs on the same machine (CPU is only ~11-16s of that). chunks.jsonl in particular is loaded in full to serve a single call site (search_knowledge.py:259, collect_official_sources) and could be replaced by a small official-source sidecar or a sqlite lookup. This is a P3 CLI ergonomics issue, not a P1 workflow blocker: the repo already routes both hot paths around the cold load — scripts/validate_repo.py:57 reuses one in-process SearchContext (744 fixtures in ~15s instead of ~16 min), and the mcp/sfskills-mcp server serves runtime agents from a long-lived process with lru_cache'd state that deliberately never touches embeddings.jsonl (skills.py:73-82), measured at 2.94s cold / 0.030s per warm query with ranking identical to the CLI.

refuted_claims.title: Output-quality evals cover 0.97% of skills and six of eleven domains have none at all
refuted_claims.reason:
The raw numbers reproduce, but the claim is overstated on three counts and internally inconsistent on a fourth.

(1) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY. The title says "six of eleven domains have none at all"; the claim's own pasted evidence says "admin, data, security, devops, architect, omnistudio, agentforce = 7 domains, 0 evals". The claim cannot keep its own count straight.

(2) WRONG EVAL LAYER FOR THE LENS. The lens is "Retrieval quality and evaluation". evals/README.md explicitly states golden/ tests "**output quality** ... not retrieval (which is handled by `vector_index/query-fixtures.json`)". That retrieval layer is at 100% coverage: 1356 query fixtures spanning all 11 domains and 1027 distinct expected skills — i.e. every skill in the repo has at least one retrieval fixture, including all six/seven domains the claim calls empty. Presenting "0.97% coverage" under a retrieval lens omits the layer that actually owns retrieval evaluation.

(3) AGENT EVALS IGNORED. evals/agents/ holds 53 P0 fixtures across 28 agent slugs, including admin (field-impact-analyzer, permission-set-architect, duplicate-rule-designer), data (data-loader-pre-flight, bulk-migration-planner), security (security-scanner), devops (deployment-risk-scorer, changeset-builder), architect (architect-skill-builder) and agentforce (agentforce-builder). These grade rubric correctness + envelope well-formedness — i.e. output quality — for exactly the domains the claim declares to have "zero". "Zero golden evals" is true only if you look at evals/golden/ and nowhere else.

(4) AGENT NUMBER MIS-ATTRIBUTED. "Agent baselines cover 15 of 47 active runtime agents" double-counts: one of the 15 baseline dirs (code-reviewer) is class: build, not runtime, so baselines cover 14 runtime agents. And fixture-level coverage — the thing that actually defines an eval — is 21 of 47 runtime agents, not 15.

The residual true kernel: evals/golden/ is deliberately scoped to 10 flagship skills, documented as such ("Why these ten first" — highest-retrieval, highest-blast-radius) with an expansion roadmap in framework.md and evals/agents/README.md. A scoped-and-documented staged rollout with 100% retrieval coverage and 21/47 runtime-agent output coverage underneath it is not a P1 gap; it is at most a P3 roadmap item.
refuted_claims.corrected: evals/golden/ (single-skill output quality) covers 10 of 1027 skills across 4 of 11 domains — a deliberate, documented flagship-first scope, not an oversight. Output quality for the other domains is partially covered by evals/agents/ (53 P0 fixtures across 28 agent slugs, 21 of 47 runtime agents, spanning admin/data/security/devops/architect/agentforce), and retrieval quality — which is what evals/golden/ explicitly does NOT test — is at 100% skill coverage via vector_index/query-fixtures.json (1356 queries, all 11 domains, 1027 distinct expected skills). The real residual gap is narrower: 26 of 47 runtime agents have no eval fixture, and omnistudio has neither a golden eval nor an agent fixture. Severity P3 roadmap, not P1.

refuted_claims.title: The FTS5 tokenizer OR-joins every token including stopwords and one-letter fragments, flooding the 30-row window on conversational queries
refuted_claims.reason: I reproduced the headline symptom but refuted the causal story and the prescribed fix. Their own evidence script (scratchpad/diag.py) does not exist in the repo, so I rebuilt the measurement directly against vector_index/lexical.sqlite (130,062 chunks). tokenize_query does emit exactly the strings they quote — that part is honest. But the two tokens actually responsible for the agentforce failure, "best" and "practices", are not stopwords and are not short, so simulating the proposed stopword+min-length filter leaves the query byte-identical and the agentforce row count still 0. The counterfactual that isolates the real mechanism is querying "agentforce" alone: 29 of 30 rows become agentforce skills. That proves generic-phrase BM25 dilution, not stopword flooding. The one-letter argument is separately wrong: t* matches 75% of the corpus, which is precisely why BM25 IDF makes it harmless rather than dominant. And the decisive result is that their fix inverts on their own second example — stripping why/can/t/my/this evicts the correct target skill (security/record-access-troubleshooting, rank 5 -> ABSENT) and admin/sharing-and-visibility from the top-30, i.e. the "noise" tokens are load-bearing recall signal for conversational phrasing. This matches the repo's recorded history (MEMORY: vocabulary enrichment regressed -5%; ranking.py:12-15 warns the stopword set is tuning-locked). A real but different and smaller issue exists, so I am refuting as misdiagnosed/overstated rather than fabricated.
refuted_claims.corrected: Correct core symptom, wrong diagnosis and wrong fix. What is TRUE and verified: (1) `pipelines/lexical_index.py:12-17` does OR-join every token as a prefix with no stopword list and no minimum length, and the apostrophe genuinely produces a bare `t*`; (2) `agentforce best practices` really does return 0 of 53 agentforce skills and `Coverage: NONE`. What is FALSE: the cause is NOT stopwords or one-letter fragments. The diluting tokens in the headline example are `best` and `practices` — neither is a stopword (`'best' in _STOPWORDS -> False`, `'practices' -> False`) and both are >2 chars, so the proposed remedy is a literal no-op there: after applying a stopword+min-length filter the query is unchanged (`'agentforce best practices'`) and agentforce rows stay at 0. Worse, the remedy actively REGRESSES the claim's own second example: on "why can't my sales rep see this opportunity record" the full unfiltered query ranks `security/record-access-troubleshooting` at #5 and surfaces `admin/sharing-and-visibility`, while the stopword-stripped form drops BOTH out of the top-30 entirely. The `t*` fragment is also not a flooder in practice — it prefix-matches 97,085/130,062 chunks, which gives it near-zero BM25 IDF weight, and FTS5 `ORDER BY bm25()` discounts it automatically. The real, narrower issue is generic multi-word domain phrases ("best practices") whose chunk-level BM25 mass outweighs a single high-IDF entity token inside a 30-row window; the fix would be entity/IDF-aware term weighting or a required-term (AND) clause for rare tokens, not stopword removal. Note also `pipelines/ranking.py:12-15` carries an explicit warning that the stopword set is tuning-locked to a measured +15pp held-out Hit@1 result, so blindly reusing it in the FTS path is contraindicated. Severity is below P1: the corpus-wide measured baseline is Hit@1 95.0% / Hit@3 98.8% (config/retrieval-config.yaml).

refuted_claims.title: Industry-cloud and error-catalog skills act as retrieval attractors, capturing generic queries that belong to core skills
refuted_claims.reason:
OVERSTATED. Their evidence command is unreproducible — `scratchpad/harness.py` does not exist in the repo (`ls: scratchpad/: No such file or directory`), so I re-ran every query through `scripts/search_knowledge.py`. Results split three ways.

REAL (2 of 5): A07 "clean up duplicate accounts in our org" -> admin/npsp-household-accounts (1.718), data/clinical-data-quality (0.634); D04 "write a test class that gets 100% coverage on my trigger handler" -> apex/npsp-trigger-framework-extension (1.120) with apex/test-class-standards nowhere in the top-10 chunks. Those two misses reproduce.

But the claim's supporting cases collapse:

(a) "absent" is factually wrong for A07. `skills/admin/duplicate-management/references/gotchas.md [0.482]` and `.../examples.md [0.399]` are BOTH in the returned chunk list (ranks 4 and 6). The skill is retrieved and shown to the consumer; it is only filtered out of the aggregated "Top skills" header by the coverage gate (`min_skill_score: 1.5` OR `min_skill_max_score: 1.0`). "Absent from retrieval" != "below the confidence gate".

(b) E02 is not a hijack — it is the correct answer. apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis has a dedicated `references/error-codes.md` entry titled `### INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS_ON_CROSS_REFERENCE_ENTITY` plus `security-sharing.md` coverage, and its frontmatter explicitly declares `'INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS'` as a trigger keyword. `grep -rl INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS_ON_CROSS_REFERENCE_ENTITY skills/` returns only 5 files; the other 4 (apex-execute-anonymous gotchas, flow-debugging, api-error-handling-design examples) are passing mentions. There is no "skill that actually fixes it" being crowded out — the claim names none, and none exists with deeper coverage.

(c) T02 contradicts its own pasted evidence. The claim text says netsuite "surfaces admin/fsl-inventory-management"; their own output line reads `T02 ... -> []`. Under their harness the result was EMPTY (correctly gated), not a vertical hijack.

(d) The framing "industry-cloud skills act as attractors" is presented as a discovery, but this exact failure mode is already diagnosed and actively tuned in the repo. `config/retrieval-config.yaml` documents: "Chunk-level lexical scoring cannot tell 'this skill is ABOUT X' from 'this skill MENTIONS X', so niche/adjacent skills outranked foundational ones ('create a validation rule' returned data/data-migration-planning)" — and adds `name_match_weight: 1.5` / `description_match_weight: 0.5`, swept 2026-07-31 against a 20-query held-out set and 400-fixture sample. There is also a measurement harness (`evals/measurement/realistic_queries.json`, 71 hand-crafted phrasings, run_realistic_smoke.py) already tracking realistic-phrasing Hit@1 at 78.9%.

So: a genuine 2-query symptom, mislabeled as a P1 two-pattern systemic defect, with the error-catalog half wrong, one case self-contradicted, and the root cause already an owned/tuned knob.

This is an instance of the already-documented "ABOUT X vs MENTIONS X" ranking problem that `config/retrieval-config.yaml` addresses with name_match_weight/description_match_weight, not a new class of defect. refuted_claims.lens: Salesforce Platform Coverage Gaps (2026 platform surface vs. library inventory)
refuted_claims.title: The Spring '26 / Summer '26 Agentforce platform surface (Multi-Agent Orchestration, Agentforce in Flow, Agentforce DX MCP server / Vibe IDE, Setup with Agentforce) is absent
refuted_claims.reason:
The evidence command reproduces, and 4 of the 6 named features do have zero SKILL.md coverage — so a real gap exists. But the claim as written is overstated on its two headline items, which is enough to refute it as stated.

(1) Multi-Agent Orchestration is NOT "prose in 3 architecture skills, never a build skill." skills/architect/ai-platform-architecture/ treats it as a first-class deliverable: "multi-agent orchestration" and "Supervisor agent topology" are declared trigger keywords in its frontmatter description; SKILL.md has a dedicated "### Multi-Agent Supervisor/Specialist Topology" section defining Supervisor / Specialist / handoff contracts and cites the Salesforce Architects Enterprise Agentic Architecture guide; templates/ai-platform-architecture-template.md ships a fill-in "### Supervisor Agent" design block (model assigned, scope, non-overlapping topic descriptions); references/llm-anti-patterns.md has "Anti-Pattern 3: Designing Multi-Agent Topology with Shared Actions on the Supervisor." search_knowledge.py ranks it 1.649 as top skill for "multi-agent orchestration supervisor agent routing." Additionally skills/agentforce/agentforce-agent-handoff-patterns/ is an agentforce-domain skill whose declared triggers include "agent to agent handoff pattern" and which specifies trigger → context package → user message → receiver ack → hand-back for agent-to-agent transfers. The topology and handoff contract layer is covered; what is genuinely missing is only the Spring '26 *declarative* Multi-Agent Orchestration build surface (agent-as-action wiring in Agent Builder).

(2) The claim's own severity/scope is inflated by counting items its evidence command never established (Agentforce Voice, Tableau MCP appear in the probe output but not in the claim body), and by counting Agentforce Vibes IDE — which is also documented in docs/comparison.md and registered in standards/salesforce-vocabulary.json ("Vibes": ["agentforce vibes", "salesforce vibes"]), i.e. it is a known/tracked term, not invisible.

(3) The MCP sub-claim conflates two things. skills/agentforce/salesforce-mcp-server-setup/ and skills/agentforce/mcp-tool-definition-apex/ exist, and the former explicitly scopes itself OUT of hosted/Agentforce-native MCP. So "the Agentforce DX MCP Server has 1 passing mention" is true, but the MCP surface generally is covered; only the DX/local-dev server is not. BACKLOG.yaml line 957 shows an intake was already triaged as "COVERED" against salesforce-mcp-server-setup, meaning this area has been deliberately assessed rather than overlooked.

What survives as a real gap, at lower severity: Agentforce in Flow Builder (0 hits; none of the 63 skills/flow/ packages mention it), Setup with Agentforce (0), Help Agent / portal self-service (0), Agentforce DX MCP server / local agent dev loop (0), and the declarative Multi-Agent Orchestration build steps. That is a P2 "newest-release build-surface lag," not a P1 "the platform surface is absent" — the 53 agentforce skills plus architect/ai-platform-architecture already carry the topology, handoff, MCP, and governance concepts these features sit on top of.
refuted_claims.corrected: Four Spring '26 / Summer '26 Agentforce *build surfaces* have no dedicated skill: Agentforce in Flow Builder (0 SKILL.md hits across all 63 skills/flow/ packages), Setup with Agentforce (0), Help Agent / portal self-service (0), and the Agentforce DX MCP server + Vibes local dev loop (0 for "Agentforce DX MCP"; Vibes has 1 LWC mention plus a docs/comparison.md reference and a standards/salesforce-vocabulary.json entry). Multi-Agent Orchestration should be REMOVED from the gap: architect/ai-platform-architecture declares "multi-agent orchestration" as a trigger and ships a Supervisor/Specialist SKILL.md section, a Supervisor Agent design template block, and a dedicated anti-pattern, and agentforce/agentforce-agent-handoff-patterns covers agent-to-agent handoff contracts; only the declarative agent-as-action wiring in Agent Builder is uncovered. MCP generally is covered by agentforce/salesforce-mcp-server-setup and agentforce/mcp-tool-definition-apex. Severity P2, not P1.

refuted_claims.corrected: Narrow residual gap, not P1 staleness. refuted_claims.title: No release-tracking mechanism: 972/1027 skills pinned to "Spring '25+", 32 have a malformed version string, and nothing links skills to release notes
refuted_claims.reason: The headline assertions are false. (1) "There is no per-skill or repo-level process that re-validates content against each seasonal release" — a full mechanism is specified and committed: `agents/currency-monitor/AGENT.md` (a build-class agent whose entire job is "Watches Salesforce release notes (3 major releases per year: Spring, Summer, Winter) and flags skills whose content may be stale", with a 6-step orchestration plan, priority heuristics, and anti-patterns), plus `CONTRIBUTING.md:246` "To run the Currency Monitor for a full release scan". (2) "nothing links skills to release notes" — `standards/skill-content-contract.md` Gate 5 (Freshness) mandates release-qualified claims, deprecation banners, `[STALE-RISK]` tags and Currency Monitor triage; `standards/source-hierarchy.md:38,41,115-123,168,189` makes Release Notes the top Tier-1 source that beats older Tier-1 docs, with an explicit Currency Monitor clause; `agents/orchestrator/AGENT.md:177,185` gives Currency Monitor HIGH-priority rows queue precedence; `agents/_shared/harnesses/audit_harness/classifiers/org_drift.md:40` defines `DRIFT_STALE_SKILL` P2, which compares a skill's `salesforce-version` against the org's current release and routes to `currency-monitor`. (3) The residual defect the claim gestures at is already self-identified and dated TODAY in `BACKLOG.md:66-77`: "Status (2026-07-31): Half built. `agents/currency-monitor/AGENT.md` exists, but nothing runs it — no file under `.github/` or `.githooks/` references the agent... Work needed: A scheduled run (GitHub Actions cron...) plus `[STALE-RISK]` tag automation and a triage owner." So the true state is "designed, documented, prioritized, not yet scheduled" — not "no mechanism". (4) "malformed version string" is overstated: `"Spring '25+'"` is valid YAML that round-trips to the string `Spring '25+'`; it is a cosmetic stray apostrophe, not a parse failure. `config/skill-frontmatter.schema.json` does constrain the field (`{"type":"string","minLength":4}`), it just doesn't enforce a season regex. (5) Their own counts no longer reproduce: 823/2026-04 and 64/2026-07, not 826/61 — the library is actively being touched in the current month, undercutting "set once and never advanced". Severity is at most P3 (unscheduled automation for an already-specified process), not P1.
refuted_claims.corrected: The release-currency process exists and is documented — `agents/currency-monitor/AGENT.md` (release-notes scan → `[STALE-RISK]` annotation → UPDATE queue rows), Gate 5 "Freshness" in `standards/skill-content-contract.md`, the Release-Notes-wins precedence rule in `standards/source-hierarchy.md`, and the `DRIFT_STALE_SKILL` classifier in the audit harness — but it is human-invoked only: no `.github/workflows/` or `.githooks/` entry schedules it, `[STALE-RISK]` appears in 0 skills, `/check-currency` has no file in `commands/`, and the agent still writes to `MASTER_QUEUE.md` rather than `BACKLOG.yaml`. `validate_repo.py` also does not regex-validate `salesforce-version` (the JSON schema only enforces `minLength: 4`), which is why 32 skills carry the cosmetically-odd-but-valid value `Spring '25+'`. This is a wiring/scheduling gap the repo already logs in `BACKLOG.md` ("Source staleness monitoring (Currency Monitor) — Half built", dated 2026-07-31) with a stated deferral rationale, so it is P3 housekeeping, not a P1 missing capability.

refuted_claims.corrected: Not a platform-coverage gap.
